# §18D · THE LADDER IS A DEFAULT, NOT A RULE ⭐ *(owner, T473)*

## 18D.1 ⭐ EVERY SETTING IN §18C IS A DEFAULT THE CLIENT CAN CHANGE

**Confirmed: the four rungs, the order, the intervals and the stop rules ship as
defaults — and the client designs their own process from there.**

⭐ **This needs no new machinery, because §14.7 already built it.** The ladder is
a **plan**, and a plan is what the automation canvas draws. So the client:

| Wants to | Does |
| :--- | :--- |
| Drop a rung — *"never call, email only"* | deletes the node |
| Reorder — *"call first, they're a phone business"* | drags it |
| Retime — *"one day, not three"* | edits the wait |
| Add a rung — SMS, a second email, a LinkedIn touch | drops in any action from the ~1,640 |
| Branch — *"if they opened the email, call within the hour"* | adds a condition |
| Change the stop rule | edits it |
| Or just talk to it | *"stop calling people who opened the email twice"* — the assistant edits the same plan (§14.7) |

⛔ **What stays fixed, because it is correctness rather than preference:**

- **One `Conversation` across every rung.** A client can restructure the ladder;
  they cannot un-join the thread.
- **`Person.state` still advances only on their own act** (§11.2). No rung
  promotes a prospect by being sent.
- **AMD still treats uncertain as human** (§18C.4). Not a preference.

### The starter library

The default ladder ships as one of several templates, so a client picks a shape
before they edit one:

| Template | Shape |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Standard** *(default)* | form → email → voice → voicemail |
| **Email-first** | email → email → form |
| **Phone-first** | voice → voicemail → email |
| **Light touch** | form → email, stop |
| **Blank** | build it from nothing |

⭐ **Same pattern as the 200 page templates and the 100 industry profiles: a
running start they own from minute one, not a wizard they have to finish.**

## 18D.2 ⭐ THE METERING LAW — DELIVERY vs THINKING

**Form outreach debits AI credits.** Generalising that to the rule it implies:

> ⭐ **The channel meters the delivery. AI credits meter the thinking.**

| Work | Meter |
| :--- | :--- |
| Discovering the prospect | **lead credits** |
| Researching them, composing the proposal | ⭐ **AI credits** |
| **Submitting a form** | ⭐ **AI credits** — there is no carrier, the work *is* the thinking |
| Sending the email | **email meter** + AI credits for the composition |
| Placing the call | **voice meter** (per minute) + AI credits for the conversation |
| Dropping the voicemail | **voice meter** + AI credits for the script and speech |
| A blocked scrape | ⛔ **nothing** — three attempts cost us bandwidth, never the tenant (§18B.1) |

**Why this is the right split, and not just a billing convenience:** it means a
client always knows *what they are paying for*. A form submission has no carrier
cost, so charging a "message" for it would be inventing a fee. It has real AI
cost — research, composition, field mapping — so it debits AI. ⭐ **The meter
matches the work, which is why the bill is explainable** — and `EXPLAIN` (§14.3)
can say exactly that when asked.

**All five meters auto top-up** (§17.6). A ladder never stalls mid-sequence
because a balance emptied.

## 18D.3 WHAT THIS ADDS

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **New modules** | **none.** The canvas already renders plans; the ladder is a plan. **229 holds** |
| **New content** | 5 starter ladder templates → the content register (§7B.2), authored at K2 |
| **Actions** | ~4 — `outreach.template.apply` · `outreach.ladder.clone` |
| **Law added** | ⭐ **the channel meters delivery, AI credits meter thinking** |

⭐ **The structural win, stated once:** because the ladder is a plan and the canvas
edits plans, **a client's custom outreach process is not a feature we build for
them — it is the same object our default ships as.** There is no "advanced mode",
no second engine, and nothing they can draw that the assistant can't also explain.

# §18E · ⭐ THE COMPLETE METER TABLE *(owner, T474)*

## 18E.1 THE UNIVERSAL RULE

> ⭐ **Everything debits AI credits. The channel meter is *in addition*, never
> instead.**

This supersedes any reading of §18D.2 where a channel meter replaced the AI
debit. **Both always fire** — the thinking and the delivery are two costs and the
tenant sees both.

| Work | AI credits | Plus |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| Discover a prospect | ✅ | **lead credits** — 1 per record |
| Research + compose a proposal | ✅ | — |
| **Submit a form** | ✅ | — *(no carrier)* |
| Send an SMS / MMS / RCS | ✅ | **1 message** |
| Send an email | ✅ | **1 send** |
| **Voice call or voicemail drop** | ✅ | ⭐ **$0.07 / minute** |
| Blocked scrape *(3 attempts)* | ⛔ nothing | ⛔ nothing |

⭐ **Two lines on the bill, always: what it thought, and what it delivered.** That
is what makes `EXPLAIN` (§14.3) able to answer *"why did this campaign cost
that?"* with a real breakdown instead of a category.

## 18E.2 VOICE — THE NUMBERS

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Rate** | ⭐ **$0.07 per AI voice minute** |
| **Included** | **100 minutes / month** |
| **Top-up** | **$100 → $100 credit** *(≈1,430 minutes)* |
| **Volume top-up** | ⭐ **$300 → $400 credit** *(≈5,715 minutes — a 33% bonus)* |
| **Behaviour** | auto top-up on exhaustion, like every meter (§17.6) |

**Every figure lives in the rate registry.** They appear here once for the
engineering consequence below, and the registry is the only source a surface
reads.

## 18E.3 ⛔ THE ENGINEERING CONSEQUENCE — 7¢ FORCES THE ARCHITECTURE

**This price point is only viable on the self-orchestrated stack, and that is
worth stating plainly before anyone reaches for a shortcut.**

| Engine | All-in cost | Margin at $0.07 retail |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Retell** | ~$0.07/min | ⛔ **zero, or negative** |
| **Bland** | ~$0.09/min | ⛔ **negative** |
| **Vapi** | $0.05 orchestration **+ providers** | ⛔ thin to negative once STT/LLM/TTS land |
| ⭐ **LiveKit self-orchestrated** — our own STT, LLM and TTS selection, per-component | **~$0.03–0.05** with the M2 confidence router | ✅ **workable** |

> ⭐ **The pricing decision and the M1 architecture decision are the same
> decision.** M1 already specced LiveKit transport with Pipecat-shaped pipeline
> control precisely so barge-in and component selection are ours. **At 7¢, a
> managed voice provider is not an option — it is a loss per minute.**

**Three levers that keep it workable, all already in the plan:**

1. **Confidence routing (§16.5)** — a small model answers, escalating only when
   unsure. Most voice turns are simple.
2. **Single-pass retrieval (§16.0)** — no agentic loop on the voice path. The
   ruling that protects latency also protects margin.
3. **Per-component provider choice** — Cartesia (~40ms) or ElevenLabs Flash
   (~75ms) on TTS, chosen per tenant tier rather than bundled by a vendor.

⚠️ **The number to watch:** all-in cost per minute, reported per tenant and per
model, on the same dashboard as latency. **If cost/minute rises above ~$0.05 the
margin is gone before anyone notices**, so it is an alert, not a monthly report.

## 18E.4 WHERE THE MARGIN ACTUALLY LIVES

Stating this once so nobody prices the wrong thing later:

| Meter | Margin shape |
| :--- | :--- |
| **AI credits** | ⭐ **8:1** — the primary margin (§17.6) |
| **Lead credits** | ~$5–10/1K retail on cheap-first fetching (§18A.1) |
| **SMS / email** | carrier and ESP pass-through with a small spread |
| **Voice** | ⭐ **near cost, deliberately** |

⭐ **Voice at 7¢ is an acquisition lever, not a profit centre** — it is the number
that makes *"an AI answers your phone"* an easy yes, and every answered call
generates AI credits, lead records, review invites and jobs. **The call is the
door; the platform is the business.**

## 18E.5 WHAT THIS ADDS

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **New modules** | **none. 229 holds** |
| **Registry rows** | voice rate · included minutes · two top-up tiers with the volume bonus |
| **New alert** | ⭐ `voice.cost_per_minute.high` — fires above ~$0.05 all-in, per tenant per model |
| **Law added** | ⭐ **everything debits AI credits; the channel meter is additional** |
| **Constraint recorded** | ⛔ **7¢ requires self-orchestration.** A managed voice engine loses money per minute |

# §18F · ⭐ THE VOICE STACK — CHEAPEST-FIRST, THREE TIERS *(owner, T475)*

**LiveKit is the transport in every tier. What changes is where the STT, LLM and
TTS come from.**

## 18F.1 TIER 1 — MANAGED, CHEAPEST *(the default)*

| Component | Default | Why | Fallback |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transport / SIP** | **LiveKit** | WebRTC + native SIP, self-hostable later without a rewrite | — |
| **STT** | **Deepgram** *(Nova family)* | cheapest credible streaming STT; built for realtime, not batch | AssemblyAI |
| **LLM** | ⭐ **Groq** | the lowest time-to-first-token at low $/Mtok — **TTFT is the whole game on a voice turn** | Together · Fireworks · DeepInfra |
| **TTS** | **Deepgram Aura**, or **Kokoro served** | cheap per character, fast first-audio | Cartesia (~40ms) for premium tiers |
| **Turn detection / barge-in** | **ours, at the orchestrator** | never a vendor's — §15.2 | — |

⭐ **Groq on the LLM hop is the single highest-leverage default.** A voice turn is
lost or won on time-to-first-token, and Groq's whole architecture is that number.
Cheap *and* fast is rare; take it where it exists.

## 18F.2 ⭐ TIER 2 — SPEECH-NATIVE: DELETE THE STT HOP ENTIRELY

**Ultravox** takes **audio in directly** and emits text — no separate
transcription step.

| | Tier 1 | ⭐ Tier 2 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hops | audio → STT → LLM → TTS | **audio → LLM → TTS** |
| Latency | STT adds its own | ⭐ **one whole hop removed** |
| Cost | STT is a line item | ⭐ **that line item disappears** |
| Nuance | tone and hesitation lost in transcription | **the model hears the caller** |

⭐ **This is both the cheapest and the fastest configuration, which almost never
happens.** It goes on the test bench immediately — Kokoro + Ultravox + LiveKit is
already a combination with real miles on it.

⚠️ **Test before defaulting:** speech-native models are strong on conversation and
weaker on rare proper nouns — a mis-heard street name or surname matters more here
than a mis-heard word would in a chat. Measure against the same recorded call set
CI uses for latency.

## 18F.3 TIER 3 — FULLY SELF-HOSTED

| Component | Self-hosted |
| :--- | :--- |
| Transport | **LiveKit**, our infrastructure |
| STT | **faster-whisper / WhisperX** on GPU |
| LLM | **Llama or Qwen on vLLM** |
| TTS | ⭐ **Kokoro** — open weights, tiny, genuinely fast |

⭐ **The economics invert here, and that is the point.** Managed APIs charge per
minute; self-hosting charges per GPU-hour whether or not a call is happening.
**Below the crossover, managed is cheaper. Above it, self-hosted is dramatically
cheaper.**

⚠️ **The crossover is measured, never guessed.** The dashboard already reports
all-in cost per minute (§18E.3); the tier flips when the measured curves cross,
and the flip is a config change because **LiveKit is the transport in all three
tiers** — no rewrite, no migration.

## 18F.4 THE SELECTION RULES

1. **Per-component, never per-vendor.** STT, LLM and TTS are chosen
   independently — a bundle is someone else's margin.
2. **Stored in `platform_settings`, changeable with no deploy** (§16.5). A cheaper
   provider ships as a config row.
3. **Per-tenant-tier override** — premium tenants can get Cartesia TTS without
   changing anyone else's stack.
4. **Failover per component**, not per stack. TTS down ≠ voice down.
5. ⭐ **Every rate is `[VERIFY-AT-BUILD]` in the rate registry.** Provider pricing
   moves monthly; the plan names the *choice*, the registry holds the *number*.
6. **The alert stands:** all-in above ~$0.05/min fires `voice.cost_per_minute.high`.

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §19 · M4a — THE PIXEL I  *(EXECUTED T475)*
**The tag · the collector · 16 events · the identity waterfall · the store**
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **⛔ FIRST-PASS SHAPE — PRECEDENCE (T667, §0.A):** first-pass pixel I; current §132 (M11). *Nothing here is deleted (law 10); read §0.A before treating this section as current.*

## 19.0 DOMAIN RESEARCH — carried from the earlier pass

| Finding | Number |
| :--- | :--- |
| Person-level identification | **5–20%** (US, LinkedIn-dependent) |
| Company-level (IP → org) | **30–65%**, global |
| B2B visitors who never fill a form | ⭐ **~97%** |
| Category volatility | ⚠️ **Koala wound down** — a warning, not a trend |

⭐ **The 97% is the whole business case.** Everything in M4a exists to make the
other 97% legible.

## 19.1 ⭐ THE COLLECTOR IS ON THE TENANT'S OWN SUBDOMAIN

**The most consequential technical decision in the pixel, and it is not the
identity graph.**

```
  tenant site  ──►  data.theirdomain.com  ──►  us
                    ⭐ first-party, their DNS, their cookie
```

| | Third-party pixel | ⭐ First-party subdomain |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Cookie lifetime | days, or blocked outright | **full first-party lifetime** |
| Tracking protection | blocked by default in most browsers | not third-party, so not blocked as one |
| Ad-blocker lists | listed | not a known third-party host |
| Who owns the data | ambiguous | ⭐ **unambiguously the tenant** |

⭐ **This is why the pixel keeps working while third-party cookies keep dying.**
Setup is one CNAME, verified live by the install checker (M4b).

## 19.2 THE TAG — AND THE HONESTY LOOP

`goaiez.js` — **one snippet, every surface**, ~14KB budget.

⛔ **We sell page speed. A tag that slows a site is a fraud.** So:

- Async, non-blocking, deferred until after first paint.
- **Hard CI budget on tag size and main-thread time**; a build that exceeds it fails.
- ⭐ **We measure our own tag's cost on the tenant's site and publish it** on their
  performance page, beside every third-party script we flag for them.

⭐ **Publishing our own number is the only version of this that is believable.**
A performance product that hides its own weight has already lost the argument.

## 19.3 THE 16 EVENTS — A PUBLISHED SCHEMA

| # | Event | Carries |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | `page_view` | url · page_class · referrer · title |
| 2 | `scroll_depth` | 25/50/75/100 thresholds |
| 3 | `time_on_page` | dwell, capped |
| 4 | `click` | selector · text · destination |
| 5 | ⭐ `form_start` | form id · first field touched |
| 6 | ⭐ **`form_abandon`** | ⭐ **the field they quit at** — the highest-value event we collect |
| 7 | `form_submit` | form id · captured fields |
| 8 | `call_click` | number · the `call_token` shown |
| 9 | `chat_open` / `chat_message` | widget session |
| 10 | `exit_intent` | page_class at exit |
| 11 | `rage_click` | selector · count in window |
| 12 | `video_play` / `progress` | asset · percentage |
| 13 | `download` | asset |
| 14 | `web_vitals` | ⭐ **LCP · INP · CLS · TTFB** from a real visitor |
| 15 | `error` | 404 · JS error · broken journey |
| 16 | `session_end` | duration · pages · outcome |

**Published, versioned, and additive-only** — the same contract discipline as the
action registry (§12.9). ⭐ **Because it is published, a tenant's own developer can
read it, and the automation canvas can trigger on any of the 16.**

⭐ **`form_abandon` is the one that earns its keep.** *Which field killed the
form* is actionable in a way no aggregate is — for most local sites the answer is
one field, and removing it is free money.

## 19.4 ⭐ THE SIX-TIER IDENTITY WATERFALL

Runs on **X-150** (§18.1), writing `PersonIdentity` rows — never flat columns —
so every field carries its source, confidence and timestamp (§11.3).

| Tier | Signal | Confidence | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | ⭐ **Declared** — they typed it into a form, chat, or the one-question survey | **1.00** | the best tier there is, and the cheapest |
| **2** | **Returning known visitor** — first-party cookie matches a prior identified session | 0.95 | |
| **3** | **Click-through match** — arrived from our own tracked link or email | 0.90 | |
| **4** | **Call match** — the `call_token` on this visit ties to a real inbound call | ⭐ 0.95 | *the join no visitor-ID vendor has* |
| **5** | **Person-level provider** — identity-graph match | 0.60–0.80 | **5–20% hit rate** |
| **6** | **Company-level** — IP → organisation | 0.50–0.70 | **30–65%**, global |

⭐ **Tier 4 is ours alone.** Every visitor-ID vendor starts at tier 5 because
they only have the website. We have the phone, so a caller who browsed becomes
identified at 0.95 without buying a single data record.

⛔ **Stop at the first tier that answers.** Tiers 5 and 6 cost money; tiers 1–4
are free and more accurate. **Cheapest and best are the same direction here** —
run them in that order.

## 19.5 THE STORE

```
Visit ──┬── VisitEvent[]          the 16, typed, append-only
        ├── page_classes[]        home|pricing|service|blog|contact|checkout|booking
        ├── web_vitals            field data, 28-day rolling (the §7D basis)
        ├── call_token            ⭐ the DNI join (§11.4)
        └── person_id             null until a tier answers
```

**Page classes are configured per tenant, defaulted per industry** — the 100
profiles already know that a plumber's `/emergency-drain` is a service page and
their `/about` is not.

## 19.6 DERIVATIONS — COMPUTED, NEVER AUTHORED

| Derivation | From | Why it matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Stage** — browsing → comparing → ready | the page-class sequence | *someone on pricing twice is not browsing* |
| **Abandon point** | `form_abandon` | the single most fixable thing on most sites |
| **Return velocity** | visit recency and gaps | feeds the cooling list (M4b) |
| **Dwell quality** | time × scroll × interaction | separates reading from a stalled tab |
| **Intent score** | all of the above, weighted per industry | what the alerts fire on |

⛔ **All derived, all recomputed, never hand-set** — so a changed page-class map
re-derives history rather than leaving two generations of incompatible scores.

## 19.7 WHAT M4a CONTRIBUTES

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Actions** | ~55 |
| **Events** | 16 published + 4 internal |
| **New modules** | **none** — X-110 · X-13 · X-132 already numbered. **229 holds** |
| **Register lines drained** | ~30 *(cumulative 280)* |
| **Seams** | 7 — `visit→person` *(identity resolved ⇒ prior anonymous visits back-attributed)* · `visit→asset` · `visit→conversation` · `visit→attribution` |

⭐ **The compounding line:** because the collector is first-party and tier 4
exists, **our identification improves every time the phone rings** — and a
competitor's does not, because they never had the call.

## 19.8 ACCEPTANCE — M4a

☐ Collector on the tenant's own subdomain, one CNAME, first-party
☐ Tag ~14KB, async, **CI budget on size and main-thread time**
☐ ⭐ Our own tag cost measured and published to the tenant
☐ 16 events published, versioned, additive-only
☐ Six-tier waterfall on X-150, `PersonIdentity` rows, stop at first answer
☐ ⭐ Tier 4 call-match wired to `call_token`
☐ Page classes per tenant, defaulted from the 100 profiles
☐ Derivations computed and re-derivable, never authored
☐ Web vitals as field data on the 28-day basis

**All nine ✅ — M4a EXECUTED.**

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §20 · M4b — THE PIXEL II  *(EXECUTED T476)*
**The panel · alerts + the conversation layer · install · outcomes · the demand index**
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **⛔ FIRST-PASS SHAPE — PRECEDENCE (T667, §0.A):** first-pass pixel II; current §132. *Nothing here is deleted (law 10); read §0.A before treating this section as current.*

## 20.0 ⭐ THE RELAY — CONFIRMED, AND IT IS THE ENABLER

```
  tenant site ──► data.theirdomain.com ──► ⭐ us
                  first-party collection      the aggregate
```

**Always first-party at the collection point. Always relayed to us.**

⭐ **That relay is what makes X-130 possible.** A single tenant's pixel sees one
town and one trade. The fleet sees every town and every trade — which is a
capability no single-tenant tool can have at any price, and it arrives as a
by-product of the architecture rather than as a project.

⛔ **What relays: counters and the tenant's own records.** The Demand Index is
built from **aggregate counters** (§20.5) — never a contact crossing from one
tenant to another. *An engineering boundary, and the reason the aggregate is
defensible.*

---

## 20.1 THE PANEL — FOUR VIEWS, ALL WORKING LISTS

⛔ **Not a dashboard. Four lists a person acts on.**

| View | Shows | Action on every row |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **LIVE** | who is on the site *right now*, what page, how long | ⭐ **call · text · open chat** |
| **TODAY** | every identified visitor today, ranked by intent | call · text · add to CRM · dismiss |
| ⭐ **COOLING** | **everyone who was hot and went quiet** | the highest-value list in the product |
| **ABANDONED FORMS** | who started, ⭐ **which field they quit at** | one-tap recovery message |

⭐ **COOLING is the view that earns the subscription.** Live is a novelty a tenant
checks twice. **Cooling is a list of people who wanted something last week and
nobody followed up** — computed from return velocity and recency (§19.6), and it
refills itself every day without anyone building a report.

Every row carries the **visit story** — *"3 visits · pricing twice · started the
quote form, quit at 'postcode'"* — and a ⭐ **suggested opener** drafted from it.

## 20.2 ⭐ X-153 `AlertConversations` — THE ALERT IS A CONVERSATION *(NEW)*

Costed separately in the harvest at ~9 lane-days, and it deserves it: **an alert
nobody can act on from their phone is a notification, not a tool.**

```
  intent threshold crossed
        │
        ▼
  alert → SMS / email / push       "Acme Roofing is on your pricing page. 3rd visit."
        │
        ▼
  ⭐ the owner REPLIES with a code       "C" → call them now
                                        "T" → text them
                                        "S" → snooze 2 hours
                                        "X" → not interested, stop alerting
        │
        ▼
  the action runs. ⭐ No app, no login, no dashboard.
```

### The code scheme — and the defect it avoids

⭐ **Five characters, never reused inside the TTL window.** A short or recycled
code routes one visitor's reply into another visitor's conversation — a defect
that is invisible in testing and obvious in production. **Five characters and a
non-reuse window** cost nothing and remove the class entirely.

### Alert rules — because a 3 a.m. alert is either revenue or noise

| Setting | Per |
| :--- | :--- |
| Threshold — what counts as hot | tenant × industry default |
| ⭐ **Hours** | tenant × alert class — *an emergency plumber wants 3 a.m.; a B2B consultancy does not* |
| Recipients + routing | role, round-robin, or all |
| **Escalation** | unacknowledged in N minutes → the next recipient |
| Rate cap | ⭐ **alert fatigue kills the feature faster than a bug does** |
| Digest fallback | below threshold, rolled into the daily |

⭐ **Every alert is a `Conversation`** (§11.5) — so the reply, the resulting call,
and the customer's own later text all sit on one thread. **The alert and the
outcome are never two records.**

## 20.3 INSTALL — THE LIVE CHECKER IS THE MODULE

⛔ **Install is where pixel products die.** A tenant who cannot confirm it is
working assumes it is not.

**The checker tests, live, and says which one failed:**

☐ `data.theirdomain.com` resolves and serves — the CNAME is right
☐ Tag loads on the pages we expect, ⭐ **and on the ones we don't** *(missing from checkout is the classic)*
☐ Events arriving — count in the last 60 seconds
☐ Cookie is genuinely first-party
☐ ⭐ Tag within its performance budget **on their site, not ours**
☐ Web vitals reporting
☐ `call_token` swapping correctly on the pages with numbers

**Per-platform recipes:** WordPress *(plugin, one click)* · Shopify · Wix ·
Squarespace · Webflow · GTM · raw HTML. ⭐ **And the AI walks them through the one
that matches** — it reads the checker output and says the next step in plain
words, rather than handing over a docs link.

## 20.4 INGEST & OUTCOMES — CLOSING THE LOOP FROM OUTSIDE

**`POST /outcomes`** — the tenant's other systems tell us what happened.

```
POST /outcomes  { call_token | person_id, outcome, value_minor, occurred_at }
```

⭐ **This is how the loop closes for a tenant whose invoicing lives elsewhere.**
They post the completed job and its value; we join it to the visit, the call, the
page and the campaign — and `Asset.earns_calls` and the attribution graph light up
without us owning their accounting.

- Idempotent by key. Retries are safe.
- Server-side ingest for anything that cannot run JS.
- ⭐ **The same endpoint feeds `X-139 OfflineConversionSync`** — the completed job
  pushed back to Google and Meta, which is what makes a tenant's ad spend actually
  optimise.

## 20.5 ⭐ X-130 `DemandIndex` — WHAT THE FLEET KNOWS

Aggregate counters across every tenant, by trade and by town.

| Produces | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Demand trend** | *"Searches for emergency drain clearing in your area are up 22% this month."* |
| **Benchmark** | *"Your response time is 14 minutes. The fastest quarter in your trade is under 4."* |
| **Seasonality** | *"Boiler enquiries in your postcode start climbing in week 41. Last year you were three weeks late."* |
| ⭐ **The public report** | a genuine link magnet — the SEO stack's `F7`, and it is real data rather than a survey |

⛔ **Counters only. Never a contact, never a record, never a name crossing a
tenant boundary.** ⭐ *And the counters are more valuable than the records would
be — a benchmark a plumber cannot get anywhere else beats a lead list they can
buy from four vendors.*

## 20.6 X-131 `InterestGraph` · X-132 `PersonGraph`

**X-131** — in-market categories with **six age buckets**, so *"looking at boilers,
first seen 3 days ago"* is a different signal from *"looking at boilers, first
seen 5 months ago"*. Fed by declared answers (the one-question survey — ⭐ the best
tier, tier 1) and inferred from page classes.

**X-132** — the relationships between identities: same person across devices, the
household, the company. ⭐ **Built from tiers 1–4 only** (§19.4) — the free,
accurate tiers. Provider matches inform it; they never define it.

## 20.7 WHAT M4b CONTRIBUTES

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Actions** | ~80 |
| **Events** | 12 — `intent.threshold_crossed` · `alert.sent` · `alert.replied` ⭐ · `outcome.posted` · `install.verified` |
| **New module** | **X-153 `AlertConversations`** → **230 total** |
| **Register lines drained** | ~40 *(cumulative 320)* |
| **Seams** | 9 — `alert→conversation` · `outcome→job` · `outcome→attribution` · `fleet→demand_index` |

⭐ **The line that separates this from every visitor-ID tool:** they end at *"here
is who visited."* **We end at a phone call the owner made by replying with one
letter, joined to the job it produced.** The identification was never the product;
the action was.

## 20.8 ACCEPTANCE — M4b

☐ Relay confirmed: first-party collection, aggregate to us, ⛔ **counters only across tenants**
☐ Four working lists; ⭐ **COOLING** computed and self-refilling
☐ Visit story + suggested opener on every row
☐ X-153: reply-by-code, ⭐ **five characters, non-reuse window**
☐ Alert hours per tenant **per class**; escalation; rate cap
☐ Every alert is a `Conversation`
☐ Install checker tests seven things live and names the failure
☐ Per-platform recipes + the AI walking the right one
☐ `POST /outcomes` idempotent, feeding attribution and X-139
☐ Demand index from counters; the public report as a link magnet

**All ten ✅ — M4b EXECUTED.**

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §21 · SEVEN OPEN RISKS — SOLVED  ⭐ *(T477)*
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

**§17.2 gave every warning a mechanism. Seven of those mechanisms were an
*alert* — which tells you a problem happened, and does nothing about it.** These
seven now have designs.

---

## 21.1 ⛔ RISK — THE IDENTITY VENDOR DISAPPEARS *(Koala wound down)*

Tiers 5 and 6 of the waterfall depend on identity-graph vendors, in a category
that has already lost a player.

### ✅ THE SOLUTION — three parts, and the third is the real one

**① Tiers 5–6 are provider *slots*, plural.** Multiple vendors per tier on
X-150, automatic failover on outage. A vendor dying is a config change.

**② ⭐ The tier-contribution report** — what percentage of identifications came
from each tier, weekly, per tenant.

> ⭐ **This is the early-warning system.** A vendor that is quietly decaying shows
> up as a falling tier-5 contribution **weeks before they announce anything.** We
> reroute on our own timetable rather than theirs.

**③ ⭐ The structural answer: tiers 1–4 are ours and free.**

| | If every paid vendor vanished tomorrow |
| :--- | :--- |
| Tier 1 declared *(they typed it)* | ✅ unaffected |
| Tier 2 returning visitor *(first-party cookie)* | ✅ unaffected |
| Tier 3 click-through *(our own links)* | ✅ unaffected |
| ⭐ Tier 4 call match *(the phone)* | ✅ unaffected — **and nobody else has it at all** |
| Tiers 5–6 | ⛔ gone |

**A total collapse of the paid tiers degrades us to roughly what a competitor has
on their best day.** ⭐ *The dependency is real; the exposure is not.*

---

## 21.2 ⛔ RISK — PERSON-LEVEL MATCH FALLS BELOW 10%

5–20% today, LinkedIn-dependent, and trending in one direction.

### ✅ THE SOLUTION — company-level-first, person as enrichment

⛔ **Nothing in the product is allowed to require a person-level match.**

| Surface | Works on |
| :--- | :--- |
| The LIVE list | **company** *(30–65%, global)* + page + dwell |
| ⭐ The COOLING list | **company** + return velocity |
| Abandoned forms | ⭐ **declared data — tier 1.** They typed it |
| Alerts | **company** thresholds |
| Person name and email | ⭐ **an enhancement on the row, never the reason the row exists** |

⭐ **So the product's value curve is flat against the fragile number.** If
person-level went to zero we would lose a name on some rows and lose nothing else
— because *"Acme Roofing is on your pricing page for the third time"* is already
the actionable sentence.

---

## 21.3 ⛔ RISK — SPEECH-NATIVE MODELS MISHEAR PROPER NOUNS

A mis-heard street name or surname is worse on a phone call than a mis-heard word
in a chat, and speech-native models (§18F.2) trade some of that accuracy away.

### ✅ THE SOLUTION — X-154 `TenantLexicon` *(NEW)* + read-back

**① ⭐ A per-tenant vocabulary, built automatically:**

| Source | Contributes |
| :--- | :--- |
| Service area | ⭐ **every street and locality name in it** |
| The 100 profiles | the trade's service names and jargon |
| Their own price list | product and service terms |
| Past call transcripts | ⭐ **names and terms this business actually hears** |
| CRM contacts | existing customer surnames |
| Business record | their own name, staff names |

Injected as **biasing vocabulary** into whichever STT or speech-native model is
running — keyword boosting is supported across the credible providers, and the
lexicon is the same artifact for all three voice tiers.

**② ⭐ Read-back on anything consequential.** Names, addresses, dates, amounts,
phone numbers: *"that's fourteen Ashfield Road — have I got that right?"*

⭐ **Which is exactly what a good human receptionist does.** It is not a
workaround for a model limitation; it is the correct behaviour regardless, and it
makes the limitation invisible.

**③ Confidence-triggered.** Low ASR confidence on a proper noun escalates to
read-back automatically, so the agent asks only when it should.

**Reused everywhere:** the lexicon also improves chat search, the knowledge base,
and the review-language mining — one artifact, four consumers.

---

## 21.4 ⛔ RISK — GOOGLE'S TERMS RESTRICT CACHING GEOCODED RESULTS

### ✅ THE SOLUTION — store the tenant's record, never Google's response

```
  Places response ──► extract ──► ⭐ the TENANT'S canonical record
       │                              (their Business / Location row, §11)
       └─ request-lifecycle cache only, short TTL, then gone
```

- **What persists is the tenant's own confirmed data** on their `Location` — name,
  address, hours, services. They own it; it is not a copy of Google's response.
- **Google's raw payload is never a datastore.** Short TTL for the request, then
  discarded.
- **Display geocodes come from the provider whose map is being drawn.** A Mapbox
  map gets Mapbox coordinates.
- ⭐ **This is better architecture anyway.** The tenant's confirmed record is more
  accurate than a scraped snapshot, and it is the record the AI must quote from
  (§13.6 — prices and facts never travel as copies).

---

## 21.5 ⛔ RISK — VOICE COST DRIFTS ABOVE $0.05/MIN

An alert tells you the margin already went.

### ✅ THE SOLUTION — automatic tier degradation

```
  all-in cost/min crosses the threshold
        │
        ├─► ① LLM hop shifts to the cheaper model      (confidence router, §16.5)
        ├─► ② TTS shifts to the cheaper voice
        ├─► ③ still high? ──► flag for the self-hosted tier (§18F.3)
        └─► ⭐ every step reported, never silent
```

⭐ **The same confidence router that defends latency defends margin.** Most voice
turns do not need the expensive model; the router already knows which ones do.

⛔ **Quality floor:** degradation stops before it touches latency or the read-back
behaviour. **We get cheaper, never worse** — and if the cheap path cannot hold
the quality bar, the alert escalates to a human instead of degrading further.

---

## 21.6 ⛔ RISK — PROVIDER DECAY GOES UNNOTICED BETWEEN MONTHLY REVIEWS

A waterfall provider whose hit rate is falling costs money silently.

### ✅ THE SOLUTION — ⭐ shadow sampling at 1%

**1% of requests run against the *next* provider in the chain as well**, and both
answers are recorded.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Cost** | ⭐ **1% of one tier's spend** — a rounding error |
| **Gives** | continuous hit-rate comparison, not a monthly snapshot |
| **Catches** | a provider decaying, **and a cheaper provider that has quietly got better** |
| **Also** | disagreement rate between providers — ⭐ *a field where two vendors disagree is a field whose confidence should drop* |

⭐ **This inverts the ordering problem.** Instead of trusting last month's ranking,
the waterfall reorders itself on measured evidence — and the shadow data is the
evidence.

---

## 21.7 ⛔ RISK — OPERATIONAL MATURITY CAPS AT B+ WITHOUT A SECOND HUMAN

Honest and unchanged. **But the right target is not a higher grade — it is fewer
things that can wake someone at 3 a.m.**

### ✅ THE SOLUTION — four reducers

**① ⭐ Degrade, never fail.** Every provider in every layer has a next one.
Voice, STT, TTS, LLM, enrichment, place data, TTS, email, SMS. **A provider
outage becomes a quality note in the morning, not a page at night.**

**② ⭐ The dead-letter queue is the only pager surface.** One queue, one place to
look. If it is empty, nothing needs a human. *A system with six alerting surfaces
has none.*

**③ ⭐ Runbooks generated from the action registry.** Every action already
declares its params, permission and reversal class — so *"what do I do about
this"* is generated from the same manifest as the help card, and cannot be stale.

**④ ⭐ EXPLAIN is the second pair of eyes.** At 3 a.m. the question is always
*"why did this happen?"* — and the system answers it from its own invocation log
(§14.3) rather than requiring someone who knows the codebase.

⛔ **The honest statement stands: B+, not A+.** ⭐ **What changes is the volume —
the number of incidents that require a human at all, which is the number that
actually determines whether one person can run this.**

---

## 21.8 WHAT §21 ADDS

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **New module** | **X-154 `TenantLexicon`** → **231 total** |
| **Actions** | ~20 — `lexicon.rebuild` · `waterfall.shadow.report` · `voice.tier.degrade` · `identity.tier_contribution.get` |
| **New reports** | ⭐ tier-contribution · shadow hit-rate comparison · provider disagreement rate |
| **Laws added** | see tracker 24s–24w |

⭐ **The pattern across all seven:** every one was an *alert* and is now a
*mechanism*. An alert transfers a problem to a person. A mechanism handles it and
tells the person afterwards. **With one human running this, that difference is
the whole ballgame.**


---

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §22 · AUTOMATIC · ONE DATABASE · TOTAL FORM CAPTURE  ⭐ *(owner, T478)*
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

## 22.1 ⭐ THE AUTOMATIC LAW

> **Every mechanism in this plan resolves itself. No runtime decision waits on a
> human.**

**Humans set intent. The system handles execution.** Applied to everything §21
designed:

| Situation | ⛔ Not this | ⭐ This |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Identity vendor decays | "review the tier report monthly" | ⭐ **the waterfall reorders itself** on shadow-sample evidence |
| Vendor dies | someone reroutes | ⭐ **failover fires; the report says it happened** |
| Voice cost drifts | an alert to act on | ⭐ **the tier degrades itself**, then reports |
| A source starts blocking | tune the `FetchPolicy` | ⭐ **backoff adapts, method escalates**, 3 tries then next target |
| Proper-noun confidence low | flag for review | ⭐ **read-back fires in the same turn** |
| A meter empties | ask for a top-up | ⭐ **tops up and keeps going** (§17.6) |
| A provider gets cheaper | wait for a review | ⭐ **shadow sampling promotes it** |
| Enrichment field is stale | a refresh job someone schedules | ⭐ **field TTL expires and it re-fetches** |
| A page changes | invalidate the Facts | ⭐ **same transaction, always** (§13.4) |

⭐ **The only human decisions left are genuine choices** — which package, which
ladder shape, what the business actually does. **Everything downstream of a choice
is automatic, and every automatic action is written to `ActionInvocation` so
`EXPLAIN` can say what happened and why.**

⛔ **A "review this monthly" line in any spec is a defect.** If it needs reviewing
monthly, it needs measuring continuously and acting automatically.

---

## 22.2 ⛔ CORRECTION — API DATA GOES INTO OUR DATABASE. FULL STOP.

**§21.4 designed around a caching restriction. That is superseded.**

```
  ⭐ every source ──► OUR DATABASE ──┬──► the client's view
     API · scrape · pixel · form ·   │
     call · form-fill · outcome      └──► the aggregate (counters, §20.0)
```

| | Was written *(§21.4)* | ⭐ Now |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| API responses | short TTL, then discarded | ⭐ **stored in our database as durable records** |
| Where truth lives | the tenant's confirmed record only | ⭐ **our database, attributed to the tenant** |
| Freshness | re-fetch on demand | ⭐ **field-level TTL** (§18A.3) refreshes what has aged |
| Ownership | ambiguous | ⭐ **one database, one row per fact, one owner field** |

⭐ **This is simpler and it is better.** One database means: the AI reads one
place, attribution joins one place, the demand index counts one place, and there
is no second store to go stale. The field-TTL schedule already built in §18A.3
keeps it fresh without anyone asking for a refresh.

**No exceptions.** Google, providers, scrapers, the pixel, forms, calls,
outcomes — ⭐ **it all lands in the same twelve entities (§11).** A source is a
`source` field, never a separate table.

---

## 22.3 ⭐ THE DUAL RELAY — ONE WRITE, TWO CONSUMERS

**Everything relays to our database *and* to the client.** Not two writes — **one
write, two readers.**

```
              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   capture ──►│   OUR DATABASE  (§11)        │
              └──────┬───────────────┬───────┘
                     │               │
      ⭐ the client's every view      ⭐ the fleet aggregate
      panel · CRM · inbox · reports   counters only, cross-tenant (§20.0)
                     │
                     └──► their webhooks · their API · their export
```

| Consumer | Sees |
| :--- | :--- |
| **The client** | ⭐ **everything about their own business**, immediately, in every surface — plus webhooks, API and full export |
| **The aggregate** | ⛔ **counters only.** Never a record, never a name, never a contact crossing a tenant boundary |
| **Us, operationally** | health, cost, quality — the same rows, different questions |

⭐ **The client is never waiting on a sync**, because there is nothing to sync.
Their panel is a query against the row that was just written.

---

## 22.4 ⭐ X-155 `FormCapture` — WE CAPTURE EVERY FORM, INCLUDING THE ONES THEY LOSE *(NEW)*

**Every form interaction on every page — theirs or ours, complete or not.**

| Captured | Includes |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Form start** | which form, which field touched first |
| **Every field** | ⭐ **the value as typed**, per field, as they go |
| ⭐ **Abandon** | **which field they quit at** — plus everything they had already typed |
| **Submit** | the full payload, independently of the site's own handler |
| ⭐ **Missed submit** | **their handler failed and they don't know it** — see below |
| **Their existing forms** | ⭐ **forms we did not build.** The tag attaches to any `<form>` |

### ⭐ 22.4.1 THE CAPTURE THAT PAYS FOR THE WHOLE MODULE

⛔ **Small-business contact forms break constantly and silently.** The SMTP
credential expires. The notification goes to an address nobody checks. It lands
in spam. The plugin updates and the handler stops firing. **The owner finds out
weeks later, if ever — and every lead in between is simply gone.**

> ⭐ **We capture every submission independently of their handler.** So when
> their form breaks, **the lead still reaches them** — in the panel, in the CRM,
> as an alert, and the agent can follow up.

**And we tell them it's broken:**

```
  submission captured by us ──► did their handler also fire?
        │                              │
        ├─ yes  ──► normal                └─ no ──► ⭐ "your contact form stopped
        │                                            delivering on the 4th.
        │                                            Here are the 9 leads it lost.
        │                                            They're all in your inbox now."
```

⭐ **That message is a renewal on its own.** It is also the honest version of a
product that measures things: we found a problem they were paying for and didn't
know about, and we had already fixed it.

### 22.4.2 Partial capture — the abandoned form

If they typed an email and quit at "postcode", ⭐ **we have the email.** That is
**declared data, tier 1, confidence 1.00** (§19.4) — the best and cheapest
identification there is, and it arrives from someone who was actively trying to
get in touch.

**Fires the recovery flow immediately:** the one-tap message from the abandoned-forms
list (§20.1), with the field that stopped them known.

### 22.4.3 Field-friction analytics

Across every form on the site: ⭐ **which field kills the most submissions.** For
most local sites it is one field, and removing it is free money — which is a
recommendation we can make with their own numbers rather than a best practice.

---

## 22.5 WHAT §22 ADDS

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **New module** | **X-155 `FormCapture`** → **232 total** |
| **Actions** | ~25 — `form.capture.get` · `form.recovery.send` · `form.handler.verify` · `form.friction.report` |
| **Events** | `form.captured` · ⭐ `form.handler_failed` · `form.recovered` |
| **Superseded** | §21.4's TTL-and-discard design — **everything is stored** |
| **Laws added** | the automatic law · one database · one write two consumers · total form capture |

⭐ **The through-line of this section:** one database, everything in it,
everything automatic, and **the client sees their whole business without waiting
for anything to sync.** The features that come out of that — catching leads their
own form lost, telling them a handler died, knowing which field costs them
money — are not features anyone designed. **They fall out of having all the data
in one place and acting on it without being asked.**

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §23 · ⭐ X-156 `UniversalIngest` — EVERY SOURCE FEEDS THE GRAPH  *(owner, T479)*
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> ⭐ **Anywhere a contact comes in, it collects.**
> **Three rules, and they are the only three.**

## 23.1 EVERY SOURCE

```
   CRM · email · calendar · Zoom/Meet/Teams · phone · social DMs
   forms · pixel · imports · orders · support · invoicing · webhooks
                              │
                              ▼
                  ⭐ ONE NORMALIZER  ── the three rules run here, once
                              │
                              ▼
        Person + PersonIdentity + Fact + InterestGraph   (§11)
```

| Source | Contributes |
| :--- | :--- |
| **CRM** *(any — native, API, Zapier)* | contacts · companies · deal stage · owner · history |
| ⭐ **Email** *(Workspace / Outlook OAuth)* | **everyone they've corresponded with** · signatures *(a signature block is a fully-formed contact record)* · thread subjects · reply latency |
| **Calendar** | ⭐ **attendees** — the highest-signal contact list most businesses have and never use |
| ⭐ **Zoom / Meet / Teams** | participants · registrants · no-shows · meeting titles · duration |
| **Phone** | inbound and outbound numbers · transcripts · durations |
| **Social DMs** | handle · thread · platform identity |
| **Forms** *(X-155)* | ⭐ declared fields, including partial |
| **Pixel** *(X-110)* | visits · page classes · intent · abandon point |
| **Imports** | CSV, any shape, mapped once |
| **Orders / invoicing** | purchase history · value · cadence |
| **Support** | tickets · sentiment · resolution |
| **Webhooks / API** | anything else, same normalizer |

## 23.2 ⭐ INTEREST, NOT JUST CONTACTS

**A contact is a row. Interest is why the row matters.** Every source contributes
both:

| Signal | From |
| :--- | :--- |
| What they asked about | ⭐ **call transcripts · chat · email subjects · support tickets** |
| What they looked at | page classes, dwell, return velocity |
| ⭐ **What was discussed** | **meeting titles, calendar event names, Zoom topics** |
| Where they are in a decision | deal stage · quote sent · proposal opened |
| Cadence | order history, contact frequency, seasonality |
| Sentiment | review text, support tone, reply latency |

Feeds **X-131 `InterestGraph`** with its six age buckets — so *"asked about
boilers, three days ago"* and *"asked about boilers, five months ago"* are
different rows, not the same tag.

⭐ **The category nobody else has:** *what customers actually said on the phone.*
Every competitor infers interest from clicks. We have the sentence.

## 23.3 ⛔ THE THREE RULES — AND WHERE THEY RUN

> ⭐ **They run in the normalizer, once. Not per connector.**

**That is the whole design.** Twenty connectors do not get twenty
implementations — a connector maps fields, and the normalizer applies the rules.
⭐ **Adding a source is mapping, never policy**, which is why the guarantee holds
at twenty sources as well as at three.

### RULE 1 — ⛔ NO SOCIAL SECURITY / NATIONAL ID NUMBERS

- **Detected before the write**, never scrubbed after. *A scrub-after is a scrub
  of something already stored.*
- Format patterns per region, matched on the value **and** the field name.
- **Dropped, and the drop is counted** — so a source repeatedly offering them
  shows up as a mapping error to fix, rather than silently discarding data.

### RULE 2 — ⛔ NO CREDIT CARD DATA IN THE GRAPH

- PAN detection by pattern **+ Luhn check**, so a random 16-digit order number is
  not mistaken for a card.
- CVV, expiry-with-PAN, track data: never.
- ⭐ **The only place card data exists is X-120 `CardVault`** — the payment path,
  PCI-scoped, network-segmented. **It is never a `PersonIdentity` field and never
  a `Fact`.**
- ⛔ **Free-text fields are scanned too** — a card number pasted into a note or a
  transcript is caught before the note is written.

### RULE 3 — ⛔ UNDER 18 IS REJECTED

- ⭐ **Rejected at ingest — the `Person` is never created**, not created and
  flagged.
- **Positive signals only:** a stated age · a DOB that computes under 18 · an
  explicit minor marker on the source record.
- ⚠️ ⛔ **We never infer age.** Absence of a signal is not a signal, and guessing
  from a name, a school-looking email domain or a device would be both wrong and
  worse than not asking. **A positive signal rejects; nothing else does anything.**
- Rejections are counted, never stored as a person.

⛔ **There is no fourth rule.** Everything else a source offers is collected,
normalized and stored (§22.2).

## 23.4 THE NORMALIZER

```
  raw payload
     │
     ├─ ① map to the twelve entities        (§11 — connector-specific, mechanical)
     ├─ ② ⭐ THE THREE RULES                 (universal, one implementation)
     ├─ ③ resolve identity                  (waterfall tiers 1–4 first, §19.4)
     ├─ ④ merge or create `Person`          (never a duplicate, never a second table)
     ├─ ⑤ write `PersonIdentity` per field  (source · confidence · timestamp)
     ├─ ⑥ derive interest → X-131
     └─ ⑦ emit `person.identified` / `person.enriched`
```

**Every field carries its source** (§11.3), so ⭐ *"where did this phone number
come from?"* answers with **"their Gmail signature, 12 March"** — and the tenant
can see it.

**Idempotent by source + external id.** A connector re-syncing is free; nothing
duplicates.

## 23.5 ⭐ WHAT THIS UNLOCKS

| Because every source lands in one graph | You get |
| :--- | :--- |
| Email + calendar + Zoom + phone in one `Person` | ⭐ **"you've emailed them 14 times, met twice, and never sent a quote"** |
| Interest from transcripts + pages + meeting titles | recommendations from **what they said**, not what they clicked |
| Order history + intent | ⭐ **reorder timing that is measured, not guessed** |
| Support tone + review text | churn signal before the cancellation |
| ⭐ **The whole relationship in one thread** | the agent answers as if it remembers, **because it does** |

⭐ **The line worth keeping:** most platforms have a CRM the customer has to feed.
**This one feeds itself from everywhere the business already works** — and the
identity graph gets better every time they send an email or take a meeting,
without anyone entering anything.

## 23.6 WHAT §23 ADDS

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **New module** | **X-156 `UniversalIngest`** → **233 total** |
| **Actions** | ~40 — `ingest.source.connect` · `ingest.map.field` · `ingest.rules.report` · `ingest.replay` |
| **Events** | `ingest.received` · `person.identified` · `person.merged` · ⭐ `ingest.rule_applied` |
| **Seams** | one per source, all through the single normalizer |
| **Rules** | ⛔ **three, universal, one implementation, before the write** |

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §24 · M5 — SURFACES  *(EXECUTED T480)*
**X-102 the widget · X-104 the WordPress plugin · X-129 the migration engine**
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **⛔ FIRST-PASS SHAPE — PRECEDENCE (T667, §0.A):** first-pass surfaces; current §135 (M12). *Nothing here is deleted (law 10); read §0.A before treating this section as current.*

## 24.0 ⭐ DOMAIN RESEARCH — THE MIGRATION MARKET IS SPLIT IN HALF

**Two categories exist, and they do not meet.**

| | What they do | What they don't |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **SEO migration tools** *(Screaming Frog · Lumar · Botify · Energent)* | crawl, inventory URLs, map 301s, compare before/after, preserve rankings | ⛔ **they analyse. They do not build the site.** |
| **AI website cloners** *(Wix · Webflow · Framer · 10Web · Mobirise)* | parse stylesheets for spacing, typography and palette; detect grid/flex patterns; **rebuild with modern standards so the clone can outperform the original** | ⛔ **they build. They do not preserve search equity.** |

> ⭐ **Nobody joins them. That is exactly where X-129 sits.**

**Three findings that shape the build:**

1. ⛔ **"Skipping redirects is the single biggest cause of lasting SEO damage."**
   Done properly, rankings stabilise in **4–6 weeks** — **2–3 months if the domain
   also changes.**
2. ⭐ **The redirect matrix should be generated from the crawl, not hand-built.**
   That is the join between the two halves, and it is the whole trick.
3. ⚠️ **Cloners warn: search engines prioritise original content**, so a cloned
   structure is *"a high-performance shell"* whose metadata and copy must be the
   tenant's own.

⭐ **Which resolves cleanly for us: we are never cloning someone else's site. We
are rebuilding the tenant's own site better** — their content, their metadata,
their URLs. The duplicate-content problem never arises.

---

## 24.1 X-102 · `WebChatWidget`

| Slot | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Does** | One line of JS. Answers visitors from the tenant's own knowledge, captures the lead, hands to a human when it should |
| **Entities** | `Conversation(channel=webchat)` · `Message` · `Person` · `Fact` |
| **Actions** | `widget.install.verify` · `widget.knowledge.build` · `widget.session.get` · `widget.handoff` · `widget.config.set` · ~40 |
| **Emits** | `chat.opened` · `chat.message` · `chat.captured` · `chat.handoff` |
| **BENCHMARK** | Intercom Fin ~$0.99/resolution → **included; we publish our real resolution rate** |

### ⭐ 24.1.1 THE 60-SECOND KNOWLEDGE BUILD — THE FASTEST GROUNDING PATH WE HAVE

```
  tenant pastes their URL
        │
        ├─ sitemap or crawl ──► every page
        ├─ extract ──► services · prices · hours · areas · FAQ · policies
        ├─ ⭐ write `Fact` rows with source_page + source_version   (§11.8)
        └─ ⭐ 60 seconds later the agent can answer about their business
```

⭐ **This is the single fastest route to a grounded agent in the whole platform**,
and it needs nothing from the tenant but a URL. It also feeds the voice agent and
SMS — **one build, every channel**, because `Fact` is shared (§11.8).

⚠️ **And it stays correct:** every Fact carries its `source_version`, so when the
page changes the Fact dies in the same transaction (§13.4). *A 60-second build
that goes stale in a week would be worse than none.*

### 24.1.2 ⭐ SERVER-SIDE RENDER — THE WIDGET IS SEO, NOT JUST CHAT

⛔ **A JS-only widget is invisible to crawlers.** The SEO capability list flags
exactly this — *fetch with scripts off; if the content vanishes, half the crawlers
see nothing.*

⭐ **So the widget's FAQ and answers render server-side into the page.** Which
means:

- The questions customers actually ask become **indexable content**.
- The conversation loop closes: *inbox → FAQ → page → answer engine* (§18.5).
- ⭐ **The chat widget becomes an SEO asset**, which is not how anyone sells a chat
  widget.

### 24.1.3 Conversion behaviour — from the pixel, not guessed

| Behaviour | Trigger |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Opens itself on hesitation pages** | page class + dwell + scroll — **and stays shut where people don't hesitate** |
| **Exit-intent offer** | per page class — a different offer on pricing than on the blog |
| ⭐ **Smart click-to-call** | knows if they're open; **switches to "text us" when they're not** |
| Sticky booking bar | high-intent pages only |
| Pre-chat capture | name/email before the queue, feeding tier 1 |

⭐ **All driven by X-110's derivations** (§19.6) — the widget is a *consumer* of
intent, not a second measurement system.

**Performance:** shares the tag's budget and the honesty loop — **we publish our
own weight** (§19.2).

---

## 24.2 X-104 · `WordPressPlugin` — DISTRIBUTION, NOT A FEATURE

⭐ **A large share of local-business sites are WordPress. The plugin is a
distribution channel that happens to also be a product.**

| Does | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| **One-click install** | plugin directory, then a single connect button |
| ⭐ **Adopts their existing forms** | every `<form>` on the site feeds X-155 — **including the ones their own handler is losing** (§22.4.1) |
| **Embeds the widget** | no theme editing, no code |
| ⭐ **Installs the pixel correctly** | the CNAME step is the only part they touch, and the checker verifies it (§20.3) |
| **Pulls analytics** | traffic, bounce, vitals into the panel |
| **200 templates natively** | the page library available inside WP |
| **Writes back** | schema, meta, internal links, FAQ blocks — the SEO fixes applied in place |

⭐ **The one-click that matters most:** a WordPress tenant gets the pixel, the
widget, form capture and SEO writes-back **from one install**, with no CNAME
confusion and no theme surgery. *Install friction is where every competing product
loses this segment.*

⚠️ **Plugin-directory review takes time and is outside our control** — so the
plugin also ships as a direct upload, and the directory listing is a distribution
improvement rather than a dependency.

---

## 24.3 ⭐ X-129 · `MigrationEngine` — THE HALF NOBODY BUILDS

**Crawl their existing site, rebuild it in our builder, and prove nothing was
lost.**

```
  ① CRAWL & INVENTORY      every URL · title · meta · headings · content ·
                           internal links · images · schema · status codes
        │
  ② ⭐ BASELINE            current rankings · traffic · conversions · vitals
        │                  ── captured BEFORE anything moves
  ③ REBUILD                structure detected → rebuilt on modern standards
        │                  their content · their metadata · their URLs
  ④ ⭐ REDIRECT MATRIX     generated FROM the crawl, old → new, every URL
        │                  ⛔ never hand-built. This is the whole trick
  ⑤ STAGING AUDIT          crawl the new site, diff against ①
        │                  ⭐ missing page · changed title · lost H1 · orphan → BLOCKS
  ⑥ CUTOVER                redirects live, sitemap submitted, IndexNow pinged
        │
  ⑦ ⭐ 48-HOUR + 6-WEEK    indexation · redirect chains · vitals · rankings
                           ⭐ measured against ②, so "nothing was lost" is PROVEN
```

### 24.3.1 ⭐ THE DIFF IS THE PRODUCT

⛔ **A migration that cannot prove it lost nothing is a migration nobody trusts.**

Step ⑤ compares the new crawl to the original inventory and **blocks cutover** on:
a URL with no redirect · a lost title or H1 · a dropped page · a new orphan · a
schema regression · a vitals regression.

⭐ **And step ⑦ closes it with the tenant's own numbers:** *"47 pages moved, 47
redirects live, 3 titles improved, rankings recovered in 5 weeks, LCP down 1.2
seconds."* Measured against the baseline captured before anything moved.

### 24.3.2 Rebuild, don't clone

- **Structure is detected** — grid and flex patterns, spacing scale, type scale,
  palette — and **rebuilt on modern standards.** ⭐ *Which is why the rebuild is
  usually faster than the original.*
- **Their content moves verbatim.** ⛔ We never rewrite copy during a migration —
  a migration that changes the content cannot attribute a ranking change to
  either cause.
- **Metadata preserved exactly**, then improved *after* the move has stabilised.
- ⭐ **Content improvement is a separate, later job** with its own before/after.
  Two variables, two measurements.

### 24.3.3 The honest timeline

⭐ **Told to the tenant up front, because the alternative is a support ticket in
week two:** rankings typically stabilise in **4–6 weeks**, and **2–3 months if the
domain changes too.** The dashboard shows the recovery curve against the baseline,
so week-two anxiety has a chart to look at instead of a guess.

---

## 24.4 WHAT M5 CONTRIBUTES

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Actions** | ~120 |
| **Events** | 16 — `chat.*` · `plugin.installed` · `migration.staged` · ⭐ `migration.diff_failed` · `migration.verified` |
| **New modules** | **none. 233 holds** |
| **Register lines drained** | ~45 *(cumulative 365)* |
| **Seams** | 11 — `crawl→knowledge` *(Facts, invalidated on source_version)* · `widget→conversation` · `plugin→form_capture` · `migration→asset` |

⭐ **The three surfaces share one property: they all reduce the distance between
signing up and the product working.** A URL gives you a grounded agent in 60
seconds. A WordPress install gives you four modules in one click. A migration
moves the whole site and proves it. **Time-to-value is the feature; these are the
three shortest paths to it.**

## 24.5 ACCEPTANCE — M5

☐ Research run; the split market and the three migration findings folded in
☐ ⭐ 60-second sitemap → `Fact` build, feeding every channel, invalidating on change
☐ ⭐ Widget renders server-side — the FAQ is indexable content
☐ Conversion behaviours driven by X-110's derivations, not a second measurement
☐ WP plugin: one click delivers pixel + widget + form capture + SEO write-back
☐ Plugin ships as direct upload too — the directory is not a dependency
☐ ⭐ Redirect matrix **generated from the crawl**, never hand-built
☐ ⭐ Baseline captured **before** anything moves; staging diff **blocks** cutover
☐ Content moves verbatim; improvement is a separate job with its own measurement
☐ 4–6 week timeline told up front, with the recovery curve on the dashboard

**All ten ✅ — M5 EXECUTED.**

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §25 · M6 — THE BUILDER  *(EXECUTED T481)*
**X-103 the builder · X-116 the 200 templates · X-117 commerce**
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **⛔ FIRST-PASS SHAPE — PRECEDENCE (T667, §0.A):** first-pass builder; current §135. §25A is a LIVE owner ruling (the site is the platform). *Nothing here is deleted (law 10); read §0.A before treating this section as current.*

## 25.0 ⭐ DOMAIN RESEARCH — COMMERCE IS THREE PATTERNS, NOT ONE STOREFRONT

**I had X-117 down as "mini-Shopify". That is wrong for almost every tenant we
have.**

The research is unambiguous: *sort the business into its **payment pattern** before
choosing anything.*

| Pattern | Who | What they need |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A · One-off** | retail products · bookings · gift cards · fixed-price services | a checkout |
| ⭐ **B · Invoices & payment links** | **trades · consultants · agencies · clinics · B2B · custom quotes** | ⭐ **a link, not a store** |
| **C · Recurring** | memberships · retainers · care plans · service contracts | tokenised methods · renewal handling · **failed-payment logic** · notifications |

⭐ **Pattern B is the default for most of our 100 verticals** — *"if you're a
consultant, tradie, agency, clinic or professional service, you may be better off
taking payment through payment links or invoice-based requests."* And the concrete
case from the research is exactly our customer: **a local plumbing business emails
a digital invoice to a homeowner and gets a lower processing rate when they pay by
secure link.**

⭐ **The line worth keeping:** *"The goal is not to offer every option. The goal is
to remove payment friction without creating operational headaches."*

**So X-117 is a pattern selector, not a storefront** — and ⭐ **the 100 industry
profiles already know which pattern each vertical needs**, so it's chosen
automatically (§22.1) rather than configured.

⚠️ **Noted and not defaulted: BNPL** may carry higher fees than standard card
processing and adds refund complexity. Available, never on by default.

---

## 25.1 X-103 · `SiteBuilder`

| Slot | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Does** | Prompt-to-site and drag-to-edit, on one canvas, published in one click |
| **Entities** | `Asset(type=page\|template)` · `Business` · `Location` · `Fact` |
| **Actions** | `site.page.create` · `site.block.add` · `site.publish` · `site.branch.create` · `site.test.start` · ~70 |
| **Emits** | ⭐ `asset.published` *(the invalidation trigger, §13.4)* · `asset.updated` · `site.test.concluded` |
| **BENCHMARK** | Framer · Lovable · v0 — canvas layers, branches, AI CMS, one-click publish |

### The mechanics that matter

- **Blocks are JSON**, matching the editor's state engine exactly — so a
  template, an AI generation and a hand edit are the same object.
- ⭐ **AI works on editable layers, never throwaway output.** The Framer lesson:
  output you cannot edit is a demo, not a builder.
- ⭐ **Branches for AI edits.** The agent works on a branch; the tenant reviews and
  merges. *An AI that edits live pages will eventually edit the wrong one.*
- **`@`-mentions** to reference pages, collections, styles and assets by name.
- **Responsive by construction** — stacks, grids, breakpoints — not three
  hand-maintained layouts.
- **A/B testing** on headline and layout with significance, results in plain words.
- **One-click publish** with hosting, SSL and DNS handled.

### ⭐ 25.1.1 PUBLISH IS A TRANSACTION, NOT A DEPLOY

```
  site.publish
    ├─ Asset version++          
    ├─ ⭐ invalidate Facts on the prior version   ── same transaction (§13.4)
    ├─ mint Facts from the new version
    ├─ COMMIT
    └─ then emit ──► sitemap ping · IndexNow · reindex · changelog · social draft
```

⭐ **So the agent can never quote a price from a page the tenant just changed.**
The builder and the voice agent are correct together by construction, which is
not a property any standalone site builder can have.

### 25.1.2 Design system — D1 in practice

`ui-ux-pro-max`'s MASTER + page-override hierarchy carries both languages
(§17.4 D1): **MASTER is Honest Counter for tenant-facing pages; console pages
override to God-Mode.** And its **192 industry reasoning rules** pick the pattern,
palette, type pairing and anti-patterns per vertical — so a spa and a law firm
get different systems without a designer.

---

## 25.2 X-116 · `TemplateEngine200`

**200 industry landing-page templates as block JSON.**

⭐ **Generated procedurally, not one LLM call per template.** The corpus's own
reasoning was right and worth preserving: *200 templates in seconds, rather than
hours of API calls that rate-limit halfway through.* Copy is assembled from
direct-response frameworks — *"Stop struggling with [pain]. Get [outcome] in
[timeframe]"* — filled from the industry profile.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Output** | one `.json` per industry, block structures matching X-103's state engine |
| **Design** | ⭐ the matching one of 192 industry rules — palette, type, pattern, **anti-patterns** |
| **Copy** | framework-structured, industry-specific, `[fill-me]` for anything only the tenant knows |
| **Imagery** | auto-sourced placeholders, replaceable |
| **Picker** | searchable, six family tabs *(the three-doors pattern)* |

⛔ **A price is never generated.** Prices arrive as `[fill-me]` cells that cannot
go live unfilled — the same rule as the profile builder, for the same reason.

⭐ **And the 200 templates are the same objects as the 100 profiles' pages**, so
the industry pages, the demo profiles and the tenant's own site all draw from one
library. **One asset, three products.**

---

## 25.3 ⭐ X-117 · `Commerce` — THE PATTERN SELECTOR

### Pattern B first, because it is most of our tenants

| Capability | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Payment links** | one link per quote, job or invoice. No storefront, no catalogue |
| **Invoices** | from the price list, from a quote the agent gave, or free-form |
| ⭐ **Deposits** | a percentage or fixed amount at booking — *the single most requested thing a trades business asks for* |
| **Progress payments** | deposit → interim → final, on one job |
| **Pay-by-QR** | on the invoice, on the van, on the door hanger |
| ⭐ **The agent can send one** | `commerce.link.send` is a registry action, so *"text her the deposit link"* works by voice |

### Pattern A — one-off

Product catalogue · cart · checkout overlay · gift cards · fixed-price service
purchase · inventory where it matters. ⭐ **Turned on only for verticals whose
profile says retail** — a plumber never sees a catalogue.

### Pattern C — recurring

Memberships, retainers, care plans. **Four things the research says to confirm
before launch, all built:** tokenised methods · renewal handling · ⭐ **failed-payment
logic** · customer notifications. Rides the same dunning ladder as our own billing
(M12b) — one implementation, two customers.

### 25.3.1 ⭐ EVERY PAYMENT CLOSES THE LOOP

```
  payment received
    ├─► `Job.final_amount_minor` set          ── the revenue number
    ├─► ⭐ attribution completes                page → call → job → invoice → PAID
    ├─► `Asset.earns_calls` increments          the page that produced it
    ├─► review invite scheduled                 (§13.3, on `job.completed`)
    └─► ⭐ offline conversion pushed to Google/Meta   (X-139)
```

⭐ **This is the moment the whole platform pays off in one row.** A payment is not
a billing event here — it is **the terminal node of the attribution graph**, and
the reason `Asset.earns_calls` (§11.7) can be a real number instead of a proxy.

**Money handling:** minor units, integers, never floats (§11.11). Tenant's own
gateway via Stripe Connect; funds never route through us.

---

| :--- | :--- |
| **Actions** | ~155 |
| **Events** | 18 — ⭐ `asset.published` · `payment.received` · `invoice.sent` · `deposit.taken` · `subscription.renewed` |
| **New modules** | **none. 233 holds** |
| **Register lines drained** | 52 *(cumulative 417)* |
| **Seams** | 13 — ⭐ `publish→knowledge` *(same transaction)* · `payment→job` · `payment→attribution` · `profile→template` · `template→page` |

⭐ **The through-line:** the builder publishes, and the agent's knowledge updates

# §25A · M6 AMENDED — THE SITE IS THE PLATFORM  ⭐ *(owner, T482)*

## 25A.1 ⭐ THE TEMPLATE MATCH — CRAWL, RANK, PREVIEW *THEIR* SITE

**The migration engine and the template library were two modules. They are one
flow.**

```
  ① crawl their current site                      (X-129)
        │
  ② ⭐ FINGERPRINT it
        │   page count · page types · has pricing · has blog · has shop
        │   image density · palette · type scale · tone · industry
        │
  ③ ⭐ MATCH against the 200 templates' own fingerprints  (X-116)
        │
  ④ rank the top 3–5
        │
  ⑤ ⭐⭐ RENDER LIVE PREVIEWS — **their own content, in each template**
        │
  ⑥ they pick one. It is already populated. Publish.
```

⭐ **Step ⑤ is the whole thing, and it is only possible because the crawl and the
builder share one block schema.** Nobody previews *template thumbnails* here —
**the tenant sees their own business, their own services, their own prices, laid
out five different ways**, and picks.

⛔ **A thumbnail asks them to imagine. A populated preview asks them to choose.**
For a non-designer that is the difference between abandoning the wizard and
finishing it in four minutes.

**And the fingerprint is reusable:** the same match ranks templates for a tenant
with *no* existing site, using their industry profile instead of a crawl.

---

## 25A.2 ⭐ THE AI DESIGNER — DESIGN BY CONVERSATION

**The builder's primary interface is the chat, not the toolbar.**

| They say | It does |
| :--- | :--- |
| *"make the hero darker and put the phone number bigger"* | edits tokens and blocks on a **branch** (§25.1) |
| *"add a page for emergency callouts"* | new `Asset` from the matching template section |
| *"this feels cluttered"* | ⭐ applies the industry rule's spacing and hierarchy guidance |
| *"show me three versions of the header"* | three branch previews side by side |
| *"use our van photo instead"* | swaps the asset, keeps the layout |

⭐ **Same engine as everywhere else:** the designer is the assistant (§14) calling
`site.*` actions from the registry. **There is no separate design AI** — which is
why it can also say *"your pricing page is your slowest and second-most-visited"*
in the same breath, because it can read the pixel too.

### 25A.2.1 Images — a different model, and an honest default

⭐ **Image generation runs on a separate image model**, routed independently of the
text LLM (§16.5's per-task routing already supports this).

⚠️ **But generated images are a placeholder, never the goal.** A generated
"plumber" is a stock photo with extra steps, and a local business converts on
**proof it is real.** So the ladder:

```
  ① ⭐ their own photos                    ── best. Uploaded, or harvested from their GBP
  ② their existing site's images           ── pulled by the crawl, already theirs
  ③ generated                              ── ⭐ marked as placeholder, with a prompt to replace
  ④ licensed stock                          ── last
```

⭐ **And the placeholder says so on the canvas**, so a site never goes live
looking like everyone else's by accident.

## 25A.3 ⭐ EVERY PLATFORM FEATURE IS IN THE SITE BY DEFAULT

**Not an integration. Not a plugin. Present because the page was built here.**

| On every published page | From |
| :--- | :--- |
| **The chat widget** | X-102 — grounded, server-side rendered |
| **The pixel** | X-110 — first-party, on their own subdomain |
| ⭐ **Form capture** | X-155 — including forms they paste in from elsewhere |
| **Smart click-to-call** | knows if they're open; switches to "text us" if not |
| ⭐ **The tracked number (DNI)** | X-137 — so the page that produced the call is known |
| **Booking** | the scheduler, inline |
| **Payment links / cart** | X-117, per pattern |
| **Review widget + schema** | true counts only |
| **Full schema graph** | LocalBusiness · Service · FAQ · Review · Breadcrumb |
| **Vitals reporting** | field data from real visitors |

⭐ **The consequence worth stating:** a page built here is *instrumented,
grounded, bookable and attributable the moment it publishes.* A page built in
Wix and bolted to five tools is none of those things until someone wires them —
and then breaks when one updates.

## 25A.4 ⭐ X-157 `HostingEdge` — CLOUDFLARE, ZERO-TOUCH *(NEW)*

| Provisioned automatically | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **DNS** | zone created, records written |
| ⭐ **SSL** | issued and renewed. **Never a manual certificate, never an expiry** |
| **CDN** | global cache, per-asset rules |
| **WAF + rate limits** | bot and abuse handling at the edge, before our servers |
| ⭐ **The pixel subdomain** | `data.theirdomain.com` — **the same CNAME step, done once** (§19.1) |
| Custom domains | apex and www, redirect to one canonical form |
| Edge redirects | ⭐ the migration matrix served at the edge (§24.3) |

⭐ **One provisioning step serves the site, the pixel and the migration
redirects.** That collapses the three most common setup failures — a broken CNAME,
an expired certificate, a missing redirect — into one automated flow with one
checker (§20.3).

⚠️ **Expiry is the classic silent failure**, so certificate and DNS health are
monitored and self-heal; a renewal that fails alerts before the site does.

## 26.2 ⛔ THE FULL-STACK SITE LAW

> ⭐ **Every site we build ships with the entire platform on it. Nothing is an
> add-on.**

| On every site, by construction | Not an upsell |

⛔ **This is the difference from Wix, Squarespace and every builder like them.**
There, each of those is a plugin you find, buy, configure and keep updated. ⭐
**Here they are the same system that built the page** — so the widget knows the
prices, the SEO knows the services, the pixel knows the page classes, and the
agent knows all three. **Nothing to integrate, because nothing was ever separate.**

⭐ **And it is why a site built here beats one built anywhere else on day one** —
not on design, on wiring.

## 26.3 CLOUDFLARE — ZERO-TOUCH

SSL, CDN, DNS and the pixel subdomain provisioned in one flow. The tenant points
their nameservers once; everything after that — certificates, renewals, the
`data.` CNAME, cache rules, image optimisation — is automatic (§22.1).

⭐ **The CNAME that the pixel needs is created by the same flow that creates the
site**, which removes the one manual step M5 still had.

## 26.4 ⭐ X-179 `TemplateMatcher` — "HERE IS YOUR SITE, THREE WAYS" *(NEW · renumbered T490)*

**Not "pick a template." We crawl their existing site and show it rebuilt.**

```
  their current URL
        │
  ① crawl                structure · palette · type scale · imagery ·
        │                page inventory · content, section by section     (X-129)
  ② ⭐ score all 200      layout fit · section match · industry fit ·
        │                content-shape fit · vertical rules (192 design rules)
  ③ ⭐ RENDER THE TOP 3   with THEIR OWN content already in place
        │
  ④ they pick            or keep browsing all 200, all pre-filled
        │
  ⑤ publish              full stack on it (§26.2), redirects from the crawl (§24.3)
```

⭐ **Seeing your own words in three better layouts is a completely different
decision from choosing a demo template.** It removes the imagination step, which
is where template pickers lose people — and the content is already migrated, so
"pick one" and "your site is live" are the same action.

**Match scoring uses what the crawl already produced** (§24.3.1), so the matcher
costs one extra pass over data we have, not a second crawl.

⚠️ **If nothing scores well, it says so** and offers the closest plus a blank
canvas — rather than forcing a bad fit and calling it a match.

## 26.5 ⭐ THE AI DESIGNER IN CHAT

**Design by conversation, on the same canvas.**

| They say | It does |
| :--- | :--- |
| *"make the hero warmer, less corporate"* | palette and type shift within the industry's rules |
| *"add a section about emergency callouts"* | new block, copy drafted from their own `Fact` rows |
| *"this looks nothing like my van"* | ⭐ upload a photo → palette extracted from it |
| *"I need a picture of a clean boiler install"* | ⭐ **image generated** — see below |
| *"make it faster"* | image weights, font loading, render-blocking — measured before and after |

- Runs on the **branch** mechanism (§25.1) — the AI never edits the live page.
- Every change previews with real content and is one tap to revert.
- ⭐ **Constrained by the 192 industry design rules**, including their
  anti-patterns — so *"warmer"* moves within what works for that vertical rather
  than wherever the model drifts.

### Image generation — a different model, deliberately

⭐ **Image models are separate from text models**, so image generation is its own
entry in `platform_settings` (§16.5) with its own provider, its own cost line and
its own failover. Debits AI credits like everything else (§18E.1).

- Photo-real service imagery · property and premises shots · hero backgrounds ·
  icon sets · social creative · **before/after pairs**.
- ⭐ **Their real photos always win.** Generated imagery fills gaps until a tenant
  uploads the real thing, and the panel nudges them to — *a real photo of their
  own van outperforms any generated image, and we should say so.*
