## 27.2 ⭐⭐ X-159 `SiteAuditVideo` — THE BEST OUTREACH ARTIFACT IN THE PLAN

**A personal walkthrough video, generated per prospect: here is what's wrong with
your site, and here is your site rebuilt.**

```
  ① CRAWL their site            X-129
  ② AUDIT it                    the 111 SEO capabilities · vitals from a real load ·
        │                       reviews · rankings · ⭐ form-handler check (§22.4.1)
  ③ REBUILD it                  X-179 renders the best-matching template
        │                       with THEIR content already in it
  ④ ⭐ WRITE THE SCRIPT          from the actual findings — never a template
  ⑤ RECORD                      screen capture, synthesised cursor, their site → the rebuild
  ⑥ VOICE                       the same TTS as the agent
  ⑦ HOST                        a personal page: their name, their site, the video
  ⑧ ⭐ TRACK                     watch depth is the hottest signal we can get
```

### 27.2.1 ⭐ THE SCRIPT IS REAL DATA — WHICH IS THE WHOLE TRICK

**Not a generated pitch. A report, read aloud, with a fix attached.**

> *"Your site takes 6.2 seconds to load on a phone. Google's threshold is 2.5."*
> *"You've got 47 reviews and haven't replied to one since March. Three
> competitors in your postcode reply within a day."*
> ⭐ *"Your contact form stopped delivering on the 4th. I found nine enquiries it
> lost."*
> *"You're not in the map pack for 'emergency plumber [town]'. Here's who is."*
> **"Here's the same site, rebuilt. Same words. 1.4 seconds."**

⭐ **This is why it isn't slop.** Every AI outreach video on the market generates a
*script*. **We generate a script from measurements** — their load time, their
review gap, their broken form, their ranking. The AI writes the sentences; **the
findings are theirs and they are true.**

⛔ **The honesty constraint that makes it credible:** every number is measured and
**dated on screen.** If we cannot measure it, it does not go in the video. No
invented statistics, no "up to", no industry averages dressed as their numbers.
*A single unverifiable claim would poison the whole artifact.*

### 27.2.2 ⭐ THE BROKEN-FORM MOMENT

**The line that converts is the one nobody else can say:** *"your contact form
stopped delivering on the 4th — I found nine enquiries it lost, and they're in
this email."*

⭐ **We can say it because X-155 captures submissions independently of their
handler** (§22.4.1). It is not a pitch — **it is a problem they were paying for,
already found and already fixed**, handed over before they've bought anything.

### 27.2.3 ⭐ WATCH DEPTH IS A RUNG-ADVANCE TRIGGER

**Someone who watched 80 seconds of a video about their own website is the
warmest prospect the ladder will ever see** — hotter than any email open, because
they chose to keep watching.

| Watched | The ladder does |
| :--- | :--- |
| **<20%** | continue on the normal interval |
| **50%+** | ⭐ **advance to the voice rung immediately** — don't wait three days |
| ⭐ **80%+** | **alert a human**, with the video timestamp they stopped at |
| **Shared or rewatched** | ⭐ treat as a reply. **They showed someone.** Stop the ladder, call |

⭐ **And the agent knows what they saw.** If they reached the review section, the
opener is *"you got as far as the reviews part — that's the one I'd fix first."*
**The video and the conversation are one thread**, because both are `Message` rows
on the same `Conversation` (§11.5).

### 27.2.4 Where it sits in the ladder

⭐ **The video replaces the plain email at rung ②** — same rung, same proposal
(§18C.2), rendered as a video instead of prose. Rung ① *(form)* carries the link
to it; rung ③ *(voice)* opens with what they watched.

**Cost per video is real** — a crawl, an audit, a rebuild render, a screen
recording and a TTS pass. So it fires on **scored prospects only**, not
on every discovered record. ⭐ *The scoring engine earns its keep here: the video
is the expensive rung, so it goes to the prospects the signals picked.*

## 28.2 ⭐⭐ X-160 `DocumentIngest` — STRUCTURE STAYS STRUCTURED *(NEW)*

> ⛔ **The mistake that ruins RAG for this use case: chunking everything.**
> A price list chunked into prose is a price list the agent will paraphrase.

```
  upload
    ├─ ① detect type        PDF · DOCX · XLSX · CSV · image · scan
    ├─ ② OCR if needed      scans, photos of price boards, handwritten notes
    ├─ ③ ⭐ CLASSIFY BY SHAPE
    │      ├─ TABLE  ──► ⭐ extracted to ROWS   (prices, services, hours, specs)
    │      ├─ LIST   ──► discrete `Fact` per item
    │      ├─ FORM   ──► field/value pairs
    │      └─ PROSE  ──► chunk + embed
    ├─ ④ extract `Fact`s    with source_document + page + version
    ├─ ⑤ ⭐ REVIEW SCREEN    "here's what I found — 34 prices, 12 services, 3 policies"
    └─ ⑥ confirm ──► live
```

### The rules

| Rule | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **A table becomes rows, never chunks** | so a price is *read*, not paraphrased — and the price rule (§13.6) holds |
| ⭐ **Numbers are never embedded as text** | an embedding cannot preserve "£85" |
| **OCR everything, including photos** | ⭐ *a photo of the price board on the van wall is a real upload path* |
| ⭐ **Review before live** | extraction is good, not perfect. **34 prices shown for confirmation beats 34 prices guessed** |
| **Source + page + version on every Fact** | a re-uploaded document invalidates the old one in the same transaction (§13.4) |
| **Conflicts surfaced, never merged silently** | *"the PDF says £85, your price list says £95 — which is right?"* |

⭐ **The upload path is the fastest onboarding we have after the site crawl.** A
tenant who drops in three PDFs — price list, service menu, terms — has a grounded
agent in a minute, with every price *exact*.

---

## 28.3 ⭐ THE ROUTING LADDER — TWO TIERS, CHEAPEST BY DEFAULT

> ⭐ **Cheapest capable model, always. Escalate only on evidence.**

```
  ① CLASSIFY          rules + tiny model · ~free · "is this simple?"
        │
  ② ⭐ TIER 1 — MINI   the default for everything. Cheapest available.
        │
        ├─ confident + grounded ──► ANSWER          ⭐ ~90% of turns end here
        │
        └─ escalate on evidence ──► ③ TIER 2 — LARGE
                                       │
                                       └─ still unresolved ──► ④ HANDOFF
```

### ⭐ Escalation triggers — evidence, never guesswork

| Escalate when | Because |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Low self-reported confidence** | the model knows before we do |
| **Retrieval miss** — no `Fact` answers it | reasoning is needed, not lookup |
| **Multi-hop** — the answer needs two or more facts joined | mini models drop the join |
| ⭐ **Any arithmetic** | *a quote is money; never trust a mini model with a sum* |
| **Comparison or trade-off** | *"which package suits me?"* |
| ⭐ **Complaint, negotiation or cancellation** | high-stakes conversations get the better model |
| **A booking or payment commitment** | irreversible, so pay for the accuracy |
| **Novel phrasing** far from anything seen | the classifier's own uncertainty |

⛔ **And where it never escalates: the voice path stays single-pass** (§16.0).
Latency wins there; if Tier 1 cannot answer on a call, the agent says so or
transfers — it does not stall for two seconds thinking.

### ⭐ Multi-LLM failover — the third axis

**Three independent things, and they must not be confused:**

| Axis | Question | Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **TIER** | is this hard? | mini → large |
| ⭐ **FAILOVER** | did the provider answer? | **timeout or error → next provider at the same tier** |
| **COST** | who is cheapest right now? | provider order by measured $/task |

```
  TIER 1 attempt ──► provider A  (cheapest)
        timeout 2s / error / rate-limited
                    └──► provider B  (same tier, next cheapest)
                              └──► provider C
                                        └──► ⭐ TIER 2, any provider
                                                  └──► handoff, and say so
```

- ⭐ **Timeout is a hard budget, not a hope** — 2s on chat, tighter on voice.
  A slow provider is a failed provider.
- **Failover never silently downgrades quality** — it moves sideways at the same
  tier first, and only escalates if the tier itself is unavailable.
- ⭐ **Provider order is measured, not configured.** Cheapest-that-succeeds, re-ranked
  continuously from the same shadow-sampling mechanism as the enrichment waterfall
  (§21.6).
- **Every attempt writes to `ai_calls`** with provider, tier, tokens, latency and
  cent cost — so the 8:1 retail figure (§17.6) is derived from truth.

⭐ **The cost consequence:** if ~90% of turns land on Tier 1 and Tier 1 is the
cheapest available model, **the blended cost per turn is close to the floor of the
market** — which is what makes 7¢ voice and 8:1 AI margins both work at once.

---

## 28.5 ⭐⭐ X-161 `DemoAssistant` — THE DEMO THAT KNOWS THEIR BUSINESS *(NEW)*

**When we build a prospect's demo site, we build them a working assistant on it,
grounded in their own data.**

```
  we crawled their site (§24.3) ──► services · published prices · hours ·
        │                            service area · policies · their own words
        ▼
  ⭐ their demo site gets a LIVE CS assistant grounded in THAT
        │
  the prospect asks their own assistant: "how much for a drain clear?"
        │
        └──► ⭐ it answers with THEIR price, from THEIR site
```

### Why this closes

⛔ **Every competitor's demo is a generic bot on a fake business.** The prospect
has to imagine it working for them.

⭐ **Ours is their business, answering as them, from data they recognise** —
because it is theirs. There is nothing to imagine.

| Property | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Grounded in their crawl** | their services, their published prices, their hours |
| ⭐ **It's the real agent** | not a script — the same X-124/C-Agent, so it **cannot over-promise** |
| **Refuses honestly** | *"I don't have a price for that yet — your owner would add it"* ⭐ **which demonstrates the fence better than any claim** |
| **Sandboxed** | booking and payment links are demo-mode; the demo never moves money |
| **Voice too** | the same demo can be called, on the demo number |
| ⭐ **Their gaps are visible** | *"they couldn't answer that because it isn't on your site"* — **the demo doubles as the audit** |
| **On both sites** | the crawl-based demo *and* the rebuilt version |
| **Conversion tracked** | every question they ask is a `Message` — ⭐ **their questions tell us what they care about, before the sales call** |

⭐ **And it converts to production with nothing to migrate.** They sign up, the
demo tenant becomes their tenant, the Facts they already saw answering become
their live Facts, and the SAMPLE badges come off as they confirm each one.

# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **⛔ FIRST-PASS SHAPE — PRECEDENCE (T667 · repaired T675, §0.A):** the three T485 cuts are collapsed here; the earlier cuts' unique lines are under §29.ARCHIVE below; current shape §136 + §139–§141 → finished §163; §29A/§30/§30A LIVE. *Nothing deleted (law 10).*

## 29.0 ⛔ RESEARCH — "CALENDLY CLONE" IS THE WRONG SPEC, AGAIN

**Same class of error as mini-Shopify (§25.0). X-108 was specced as a Calendly
clone. Most of our 200 industries are field service.**

The distinction, put better by the research than I would have:

> ⭐ *"A field scheduling tool has to handle the field dimension: many jobs per
> day, multiple technicians, travel time between sites, emergency calls that
> reshuffle the plan, and a customer who wants to pick a window without calling.
> **That is a different job from booking a single 30-minute meeting.**"*

And what separates the real thing from a calendar:

> *"It takes an incoming job, matches it to the right available technician based on
> **skills and location**, plots an efficient route, pushes the details to a mobile
> app, and **closes the loop with an invoice and payment**. That connected flow is
> what separates real field service management from a bare calendar."*

⭐ **The threshold at which a calendar stops working**, named precisely: *"once jobs
vary in length, technicians have different skills, travel time matters, and
same-day change becomes common, the schedule turns into **an operational control
system** rather than a simple list of appointments."*

### The five failures it names — and every one is ours to prevent

*"They lose them because of what happens between the jobs — the
miscommunications, the double-bookings, ⭐ **the technician who shows up without
the right parts**, the invoice that goes out three days late."*

| Failure | Our counter |
| :--- | :--- |
| Miscommunication | ⭐ the agent booked it, so the thread *is* the record |
| Double-booking | one `Job` table, conflict-checked at write |
| ⭐ **Wrong parts** | parts list on the `Job`, checked at dispatch |
| Late invoice | ⭐ **auto-generated on completion** (§25.3.1) |
| No arrival window | ⭐ **the agent quotes only windows the schedule can honour** — see 29.3 |

**Market context:** field service scheduling is **$7.2B in 2025 → $16.8B by
2034**. ⚠️ **And the overbuy warning:** ServiceTitan is *"quote-based, higher cost,
tied to annual contracts, with implementation fees that can add thousands or tens
of thousands"* — and *"expensive and complex if your team only needs a better
calendar and faster invoicing."* ⭐ **That is the gap: the capability without the
implementation project.**

---

## 29.1 ⭐ X-108 — TWO MODES, CHOSEN BY THE PROFILE

| Mode | Who | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **APPOINTMENT** | salon · clinic · consultant · studio · law · accounting | a **slot**, at their premises |
| ⭐ **JOB** | plumber · HVAC · electrician · cleaner · locksmith · pest · landscaping · mobile anything | a **job**, at the customer's address |

⭐ **The industry profile picks the mode** — same automatic pattern as commerce
(§25.0) and the payment pattern. **A plumber never sees a meeting-slot picker; a
salon never sees a dispatch board.**

### Appointment mode
Slot duration per service · buffers · staff-specific availability · rooms and
resources · two-way calendar sync *(Google, Outlook)* · Zoom/Meet links ·
reminders at 24h and 10m · rescheduling links · no-show tracking · deposits at
booking (§25.3).

### ⭐ Job mode — the field dimension

| Capability | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Arrival windows, not slots** | *"between 9 and 11"* — **what customers actually get told**, and what the schedule can honour |
| ⭐ **Travel time computed** | between consecutive job addresses, with traffic — not a guessed buffer |
| **Job duration by service type** | learned from completed jobs, not typed once and never revisited |
| ⭐ **Skill matching** | who is qualified for this work, from the roster |
| **Crew assignment** | one tech, two techs, apprentice pairing |
| ⭐ **Parts check** | required parts on the `Job`; flagged at dispatch if not in stock |
| ⭐ **Emergency reshuffle** | an urgent call reorders the day and **notifies everyone whose window moved** |
| **Recurring service** | quarterly, seasonal, contract — auto-generated forward |
| **On-the-way + live ETA** | text with a real ETA, not a promise |
| **Multi-day and multi-visit** | one `Job`, several visits |

---

## 29.2 ⭐ X-162 `Dispatch` — THE BOARD *(NEW)*

The research names exactly what a dispatch screen must answer:

> ⭐ *"Who is available, where are they, what job are they on, and **what can be
> moved?**"*

**Four questions, four glances:**

| Panel | Answers |
| :--- | :--- |
| **The board** | every job, every tech, today — drag to reassign |
| **The map** | where everyone is, live, with the route drawn |
| ⭐ **The movable list** | **which jobs can be shifted and what it costs** — *the one nobody builds, and the only one that matters when an emergency lands* |
| **Conflicts** | overlaps, impossible travel, skill mismatches, missing parts — **before** they happen |

- **Proximity-aware assignment** — nearest qualified tech, not next in a list.
- **Route optimisation** across the day, factoring locations, windows and traffic.
- ⭐ **Rescheduling propagates.** Move one job and every affected customer is
  notified automatically (§22.1) — *"a change that doesn't propagate"* is named as
  a core failure of shared calendars.
- **Mobile field view** — the tech's day, the job, the parts, the customer
  history, one-tap complete.

---

## 29.3 ⭐⭐ THE GROUNDING RULE, APPLIED TO TIME

> ⛔ **The agent may only offer an arrival window the schedule can actually
> honour.**

⭐ **This is capability gating (§16.2) applied to the calendar.** The agent does
not "check availability" and hope — it calls `scheduler.slot.find`, which returns
windows already validated against travel time, skills, parts and the existing
board. **If no window exists, it says so and offers the first real one.**

```
  2:14 a.m. — the call the competition misses entirely
        │
   agent answers ──► scheduler.slot.find(service, address, urgency)
        │                    │
        │            ⭐ travel-aware · skill-aware · parts-aware
        ▼
   "I can get someone to you between 8 and 10 this morning.
    Shall I book that in?"  ──► `Job` created ──► dispatch board updated
                                       │
                                       └──► tech notified · customer confirmed
```

⭐ **Nobody else's dispatch board is fed by an AI answering the phone at two in the
morning.** ServiceTitan schedules beautifully and cannot answer the call. The
answering services answer the call and cannot see the board. **We are the only
place where the thing that answers and the thing that schedules are the same
system.**

---

## 29.4 X-01 `Crm` · X-10 `Routing` · X-07 · X-08

**Pipeline** — Kanban over `Person.state` and `Job.state`; stage automations;
predictive scoring from actual close rates, not a formula.

**Routing** — round-robin weighted by conversion rate · skill-based ·
territory · ⭐ **speed-to-lead SLA with escalation**, because the first responder
usually wins.

⭐ **The CRM insights only we can produce**, because §23's ingest feeds it:

| Insight | Needs |
| :--- | :--- |
| *"you've emailed them 14 times, met twice, and never sent a quote"* | email + calendar + `Job` on one `Person` |
| *"three quotes over £2k are 40 days stale"* | pipeline + value + time |
| *"this customer is due — they book every 14 weeks and it's been 19"* | ⭐ **job history cadence** |
| *"they asked about a boiler on the phone in March and nobody followed up"* | ⭐ **call transcripts** |

**Forecasting (X-07)** from pipeline × historic close rate × velocity.
**Churn (X-08)** from booking cadence breaks, support tone and review sentiment —
⭐ *for a service business, churn is a missed re-book, and it is visible weeks
early.*

  quoted → booked → confirmed → on the way → in progress → completed → paid
     │        │         │            │             │            │        │
     │        │         │            │             │            │        └─ ⭐ attribution
     │        │         │            │             │            │           completes (§25.3.1)

```

## 29.0 ⭐ DOMAIN RESEARCH — AND THE BEST FRAMING OF THE PROBLEM I'VE FOUND
> ⭐ *"Most service businesses don't lose money because the work is bad. They lose
> it in the gaps between jobs: the tech sent across town when a closer one was
> free, the double-booked afternoon that turns into an angry phone call, the two
> hours a crew sits idle because the morning job finished early and nobody knew.
> **None of that shows up on an invoice. It just quietly bleeds out of every
> week.**"*
**That defines the module.** Not a calendar — a board that **stops
double-bookings and surfaces idle time.** *"A good-looking week view isn't the
goal."*
### The five findings
| # | Finding | Consequence |
| **1** | ⭐ **"Bad data at intake wrecks the day long before dispatch starts."** | see 29.1 — **this is our unfair advantage** |
| **2** | ⛔ **"Treating scheduling as an island guarantees you'll be re-typing customers between tools for years."** | ⭐ *structurally impossible here* — §11 |
| **3** | ⭐ **"The office board and the field app are one product."** If the tech's app is painful, *"the schedule drifts out of date within an hour and the whole thing falls apart"* | X-163 is not optional |
| **4** | Good optimisation **reshuffles the sequence**; bad optimisation *"drops one appointment into the nearest empty slot"* and creates bad route chains | 29.3 |
| **5** | Metaheuristic local-search over skills, geography and travel time raises **job-per-technician density 15–22%** *(ORTEC)*; 15–30% reductions reported broadly | the benchmark |
⚠️ Vendor-reported; validated on tenant zero before it appears anywhere (§7A.5).
## 29.1 ⭐⭐ THE UNFAIR ADVANTAGE — WE OWN THE INTAKE
**"Bad data at intake wrecks the day."** Every field-service vendor knows it and
none of them can fix it, **because they don't own the phone.**
  customer calls ──► ⭐ OUR AGENT ANSWERS  (§16.1)
        ├─ address, confirmed by read-back           (§21.3)
        ├─ the actual problem, in their words
        ├─ ⭐ access notes — gate code, parking, dog, "side door"
        ├─ urgency, from what they said
        ├─ ⭐ equipment or part hinted at, from the description
        └─ history, because the `Person` already exists   (§11.2)
        the `Job` arrives at the board COMPLETE
⭐ **A dispatcher's worst job is chasing detail somebody didn't take.** We take it
at the moment of the call, from an agent that reads back what it heard and cannot
invent what it wasn't told. **Every FSM competitor's intake is a human typing into
a form while a customer talks.**
## 29.2 X-01 `Crm` — A DISPATCH BOARD, NOT A SALES PIPELINE
⛔ **A plumber does not have "deals in stages." They have jobs on a calendar.**
| Layer | For |
| **Pipeline** | quotes only — *sent · viewed · accepted · lost*. ⭐ **Four states, not seven** |
| ⭐ **The board** | the operational reality: **who is going where, when, with what** |
| **The customer record** | every touch from all 18 sources (§28.1) on one `Person` |
**Also here:** X-10 lead routing *(round-robin weighted by conversion, skill,
territory, capacity)* · X-07 forecasting from real close rates · X-08 churn
signal from activity and support tone · stale-quote detection · ⭐ *"you've emailed
14 times and never sent a quote"* (§23.5).
## 29.3 ⭐ X-162 `DispatchBoard` — THE TWO JOBS IT HAS *(NEW)*
### JOB ONE — ⛔ never double-book
Hard constraint, enforced at write: a crew cannot hold two overlapping jobs.
Drag-and-drop across day, week and crew views; conflicts refuse rather than warn.
⭐ *A warning that can be clicked through is not a constraint.*
### JOB TWO — ⭐ SURFACE THE IDLE TIME
**The thing that "doesn't show up on an invoice."**
| Surfaced | Example |
| ⭐ **Gaps** | *"Dave is free 11:20–14:00 and there are three unbooked jobs within 4 miles."* |
| **Early finishes** | ⭐ job marked complete 90 minutes early → **the gap appears immediately** |
| **Zig-zag routes** | *"Two crews crossed town past each other at 2pm."* |
| **Idle vs busy** | who is overloaded, who has room |
| **Travel share** | ⭐ **hours driving vs hours earning, per crew, per week** |
⭐ **Every one of these is a query, not a report** — because jobs, addresses,
travel times and crew calendars are all in the same twelve entities.
### Sequencing, not slot-filling
⛔ **We never drop a job into the nearest empty slot.** Assignment **re-plans the
sequence** for the affected crew and day, scoring skill fit · travel time · time
window · priority · continuity *(same customer, same street)*.
**And it re-plans itself when the day moves** (§22.1) — an early finish, a
cancellation, a callout — **automatically, reporting what changed.** *A dispatcher
should spend the day making decisions, not asking for updates.*
⚠️ **Bounded:** re-planning never moves a job whose customer has been given a
confirmed window without asking. ⭐ *An optimiser that breaks a promise to save
nine minutes is a worse dispatcher than a whiteboard.*
## 29.4 X-108 `Scheduler` — BOOKING, AND WHO DOES IT
| Path | |
| **Customer self-serve** | real availability, real windows. ⭐ **Reduces inbound calls, which is the point** |
| ⭐ **The agent books** | on the phone, in chat, over SMS — *"Thursday morning or Friday after two?"* |
| **X-04 negotiation** | back-and-forth over email or text instead of a link |
| **Office** | drag it on the board |
**All four write the same `Job`.** ⭐ *There is no "online booking" separate from
"phone booking" — a distinction that exists in other products only because their
phone isn't theirs.*
**Built:** two-way Google and Outlook sync · Zoom/Meet links · arrival windows ·
⭐ **travel time as a first-class block, not a guess** · buffers · blackout dates ·
holiday overrides · capacity per crew per day · recurring *(nightly · weekly ·
custom · contract · ad hoc)* · skill-based routing · multi-ring · deposits at
booking (§25.3) · reminders at 24h and 1h · ⭐ **reschedule and cancel self-serve,
because the alternative is a phone call to the office.**
## 29.5 ⭐ X-163 `FieldApp` — ONE PRODUCT WITH THE BOARD *(NEW)*
> ⭐ *"If the app your techs carry is painful, the schedule drifts out of date
> within an hour and the whole thing falls apart."*
| **Today, one screen** | next job, address, one-tap navigation, the customer's history |
| ⭐ **The access notes** | gate code, parking, the dog — **captured at intake** (§29.1) |
| **On my way** | one tap → customer notified with an ETA |
| **Status** | travelling · on site · complete — ⭐ **each one moves the board** |
| ⭐ **Proof of service** | photos before and after. *The research flags photos as friction unless the workflow is built for it — so it is two taps, not a form* |
| **Parts & materials** | added on site, flowing to the invoice |
| **Quote on site** | from the price list, deposit taken there and then |
| ⭐ **Offline-first** | **a basement has no signal.** Queue locally, sync on return |
| **The review ask** | fires from `job.completed`, not from a reminder |
⭐ **The photos are worth more than proof.** They feed before/after job videos
(§27.1), GBP posts, the review ask and the site gallery — **one tap on site
becomes four marketing assets**, which is a thing no FSM tool does because it
isn't a marketing platform.
## 29.6 ⭐ WHY THIS ISN'T AN ISLAND
**The warning was: buy scheduling alone and you re-type customers between tools
for years.** Here, in one row:
  call ──► agent takes it ──► Job created complete ──► board sequences it
     │                                                      │
     │                                             field app runs it
     │                                                      │
     │                          photos · parts · completion ─┤
     │                                                      ▼
     │                              invoice · payment · review ask
     │                                        │
     └──────────► ⭐ attribution closes: page → call → job → invoice → PAID
⭐ **No integration exists anywhere in that line, because nothing was separate.**
The quote the agent gave, the job on the board, the photo from the van, the
invoice, the review and the page that produced the call are all the same twelve
entities.

## 29.0 ⭐ DOMAIN RESEARCH — X-108 IS NOT A CALENDLY CLONE
**The corpus called it `CalendlyCloneScheduler`. That is the wrong category, and
the research is explicit about why.**
**Three categories people confuse:**
| Category | Examples | Does |
| **Appointment booking** | Calendly · Acuity · Cal.com | a link, a slot, done |
| ⭐ **Field service management** | Jobber · Housecall Pro · ServiceTitan | **technician dispatch · route optimisation · invoicing** |
| **Shift scheduling** | Homebase · Deputy | hourly staff across locations |
⭐ **Our tenants are the middle one.** The distinguishing property, stated
plainly: field service scheduling *"knows about travel time, technician skill
sets, customer locations, job history, parts availability, and SLA deadlines all
at once"* — and **that connected flow is what separates it from a bare calendar.**
### The five findings that shape the build
**① ⛔ Load balancing is the actual problem, not slot-finding.**
*"When load balancing is purely manual, some crews wrap up by noon while others
run three hours over — driving overtime, technician burnout, and customers waiting
longer."* The fix accounts for **active job duration, travel time and remaining
crew capacity simultaneously, not just what's on the calendar.**
**② Route optimisation has a measurable return.** Businesses consistently report
**15–30% reductions in fuel and travel cost**, and technicians who drive less
complete **one or two more calls a day without working longer.**
**③ ⭐ The single most common customer complaint in field service is solved by one
notification:** *"your technician is 15 minutes away"*, driven by live location.
**④ Conflict alerts must fire before the error is confirmed** — *"not after a
technician shows up to discover they have two jobs at once."*
**⑤ ⭐ Job completion should generate the invoice automatically**, pulling job
details, parts and labour — because *"the delay between job completion and invoice
dispatch directly affects how quickly you get paid."*
⚠️ **And the warning worth heeding:** ServiceTitan-class systems *"can be
expensive and complex if your team only needs a better calendar and faster
invoicing."* ⭐ **So capability scales with the tenant** — a sole trader sees a day
list; a five-van operation sees the board. Same engine, different surface.
⭐ **One more, and it is ours:** *"an AI receptionist can answer calls 24/7,
collect booking information, and either schedule directly or send a booking
link — capturing customers who prefer phone calls while online scheduling handles
self-serve."* **That is exactly the chain we already own** (§29.4).
## 29.1 X-01 · `Crm` — THE PIPELINE
| Slot | |
| **Entities** | `Person` · `Job` · `Conversation` · `LedgerEntry` |
| **Actions** | `crm.contact.upsert` · `crm.stage.set` · `crm.note.add` · `crm.score.get` · `crm.nba.get` · ~60 |
| **Emits** | `crm.stage_changed` · `crm.stale_detected` · `crm.scored` |
| **BENCHMARK** | ⭐ **unlimited users on every plan** — *"you pay for the plan, not the seats, so growing your crew and growing your costs stop being the same thing"* |
- Kanban stages, drag-and-drop, stage-change automations on the canvas.
- ⭐ **The pipeline fills itself** from X-156 — email, calendar, Zoom, calls, forms
  and the pixel (§23). **Nothing is typed in.**
- **Predictive scoring** from historic close rates, weighted toward our own
  signals (§18.5).
- ⭐ **The line only we can produce:** *"you've emailed them 14 times, met twice,
  and never sent a quote."*
## 29.2 X-10 · `LeadRouting`
Round-robin weighted by rep conversion rate · skill-based · **proximity-based**
(feeds dispatch) · overflow and fallback · ⭐ **speed-to-lead SLA with escalation**,
because a lead's value halves fast and the clock is the metric.
## 29.3 X-108 · `Scheduling` — BUILT FOR JOBS, NOT MEETINGS
⭐ **A job is not a 30-minute slot.** The model:
Job scheduling unit
  service_type          → its typical duration, from job history not a guess
  duration_estimate     learned per tenant per service ⭐ (their 'boiler service'
                        is 90 minutes because theirs always is)
  ⭐ arrival_window       "between 9 and 11" — how trades actually book
  travel_before/after   computed from the previous and next stop
  skills_required       who can actually do it
  parts_required        ⛔ don't dispatch a job whose parts aren't there
  access_notes          gate code, dog, parking, key safe
  slot_class            emergency · same-day · scheduled · recurring
| Capability | |
| ⭐ **Arrival windows, not slots** | the honest unit for a visit |
| **Duration learned per tenant** | from `Job` history, and it improves every job |
| **Travel-time aware** | the gap between two jobs is not free |
| ⭐ **Conflict alerts before confirmation** | finding ④ — the error never reaches a technician |
| **Two-way calendar sync** | Google · Outlook, both directions |
| **Recurring jobs and service plans** | contracts, maintenance, care plans |
| **Reminders** | 24 h and 1 h — cuts no-shows |
| **Capacity by day and by skill** | so "can you do Thursday?" has a real answer |
| **Blackouts, holidays, leave** | including per-technician |
## 29.4 ⭐⭐ THE CHAIN NOBODY ELSE HAS END TO END
  missed call ──► text-back ──► ⭐ THE AGENT BOOKS IT, on the phone or by text
       │                              │  live availability, real window, real skills
       │                              ▼
       │                        job on the board ──► route optimised
       │                              │
       │                        ⭐ "your technician is 15 minutes away"   (finding ③)
       │                              │
       │                        job complete in the field
       │                              ├──► ⭐ invoice generated automatically  (finding ⑤)
       │                              ├──► payment link sent
       │                              ├──► review invite scheduled
       │                              └──► ⭐ attribution closes: page → call → job → PAID
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⭐ **Every competitor owns one or two links of that chain.** Podium and Birdeye
have the messaging and no dispatch. Jobber and Housecall Pro have the dispatch and
no AI answering the phone. **Nobody has the agent that books, the board it books
onto, and the attribution that closes on payment** — because that requires one
`Conversation`, one `Job` and one graph (§11).
## 29.5 ⭐ X-162 `Dispatch` *(NEW)*
| **The board** | every technician's day side by side; drag to reassign |
| ⭐ **Load balancing** | **duration + travel + remaining capacity, simultaneously** — finding ① |
| **Route optimisation** | per technician per day; ⭐ **target 15–30% travel reduction, measured** |
| **Live location** | powers the arrival notification and the nearest-tech answer |
| ⭐ **Emergency insert** | *"who is closest and free"* answered on the board, not by ringing round |
| **Conflict flags** | before confirmation, always |
| **Utilisation reporting** | per technician; first-time-fix rate; revenue per technician |
| ⭐ **Scales down** | a sole trader gets a day list, not a dispatch board. **Same engine** |
## 29.6 ⭐ X-163 `FieldApp` *(NEW)*
| ⭐ **Offline first** | *jobs happen where there is no signal.* Queue and sync |
| **The job in hand** | details, history, access notes, parts, checklist |
| ⭐ **Customer history** | *"you were here in March for the same valve"* |
| **Photos** | before/after — ⭐ **and they feed X-158's job videos and the GBP posts** |
| **Parts used, labour time** | which is what makes finding ⑤'s invoice accurate |
| **Card on file / tap to pay** | paid before leaving the drive |
| **One tap complete** | fires the whole §29.4 cascade |

| **Actions** | ~185 |
| **Events** | 22 — `job.booked/confirmed/completed` · `dispatch.assigned` · ⭐ `technician.approaching` · `job.conflict_detected` · `invoice.auto_generated` |
| **New modules** | ⭐ **X-162 `Dispatch`** · ⭐ **X-163 `FieldApp`** → **240 total** |

⭐ **The through-line:** the chain in §29.4 is not an integration between five

competitor — the reference implementation. Full feature set researched, and all of
it goes in.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Per technician | **$245–$398/mo**, up to ~$500 on the top tier |
| A 5-tech shop | **$1,225–$1,990/mo in software alone** |
| Implementation | ⭐ **$5,000 – $50,000+**, one time |

| Add-ons | Marketing Pro · Phones Pro · Pricebook Pro · Dispatch Pro — **all extra** |
| Free trial | ⛔ **none. No free tier. A contract is required to see the platform** |
| Published pricing | ⛔ **none.** Sit through a demo to get a quote |

⭐ **Per-technician pricing is the strategic weakness, and it is structural.** Every
hire raises their software bill. **Ours is per plan, unlimited users** — *growing
the crew and growing the software bill stop being the same thing.* That is a
sentence a shop owner feels immediately.

## 30.2 ⭐ X-163 `PriceBook` — THE ONE THAT RUNS EVERYTHING ELSE

Not a price list. **A structured catalogue of services, tasks, materials and
labour with margin logic.**

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Structure** | category → service → tasks → materials + labour |
| **Pricing** | flat-rate per task · cost-plus · time-and-materials · ⭐ **margin target that back-solves the price** |
| ⭐ **Good / better / best** | three options per service — **the single biggest average-ticket lever in the trades** |
| **Add-ons** | attached to services, offered at the point of estimate |
| **Zones** | price by service area where travel or rates differ |
| **Warranty terms** | per service, surfaced in the estimate and the invoice |
| **Images** | per task, so the customer sees what they're buying |
| **Versioning** | ⭐ a price change is a **new version**; historic jobs keep the price they were sold at |

⭐ **And it is the same registry the agent quotes from (§16.2), the site renders
from (§13.6), and job costing measures against (X-166).** **One pricebook, four
consumers, no copies** — which is exactly what ServiceTitan's separate pricebook
module cannot be, because their phone agent doesn't exist.

## 30.5 ⭐⭐ X-173 `AccountingSync` — BUILT AGAINST THEIR WORST REVIEW

> ⛔ *"~60% of users who mention the QuickBooks integration note that it is
> glitchy and **requires double inputs in both solutions, making it redundant.**"*

**Double entry means the sync is not authoritative. Ours is.**

| Rule | |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **One direction, declared per object** | invoices and payments flow **out**; the chart of accounts and tax codes flow **in**. ⛔ **Never both ways without a stated conflict rule** (§13.6) |
| **Idempotent by external id** | a re-sync is free; nothing duplicates |
| ⭐ **Conflicts surfaced, never silently resolved** | *"this invoice was edited in QuickBooks after we sent it — keep theirs or ours?"* |
| **Mapping reviewed once, then automatic** | services → income accounts, parts → COGS, one time |
| ⭐ **A failed sync is a dead letter, not a silent gap** | it appears on the one pager surface (§21.7) with the row that failed |
| **Providers** | QuickBooks · Xero · Sage · CSV for anything else |

⭐ **"Enter it once" is the entire feature**, and it is achievable because the
`Job` is already the single record from booking to payment (§29.5). **Their sync
is glitchy because their job data has more than one home. Ours doesn't.**

## 30A.1 ⭐⭐ THE INCLUDED-SOFTWARE LAW

> **The FSM set costs nothing extra. It is in the package.**
> **The only things that meter are the five existing meters — and they meter
> usage, never features.**

⛔ **No FSM add-on. No per-technician fee. No module tiers. No setup fee.**

| FSM action | What it costs |
| :--- | :--- |
| Build a pricebook, any size | ⛔ **nothing** |
| Dispatch a job · reassign · reroute | ⛔ **nothing** |
| Job costing, margin reports, dashboards | ⛔ **nothing** — a query is not a product |
| Inventory, truck stock, reorder points | ⛔ **nothing** |
| Timesheets · payroll export · commissions | ⛔ **nothing** |
| Accounting sync | ⛔ **nothing** |
| An LSA lead arriving | ⛔ **nothing** *(Google bills them directly)* |
| Memberships · agreements · renewals | ⛔ **nothing** |
| Customer portal | ⛔ **nothing** |
| — | |
| ⭐ **AI drafts an estimate** | **AI credits** |
| ⭐ **Send the estimate by text** | **AI + 1 message** |
| ⭐ **Agent sells a membership on the phone** | **AI + voice minutes** |
| ⭐ **The on-the-way text** | **AI + 1 message** |
| ⭐ **Field assistant answers a question** | **AI credits** |
| ⭐ **A renewal reminder** | **AI + 1 message or send** |

⭐ **The rule in one line: the software is included; only the *sending* and the
*thinking* meter.**

**Against their model this is the whole argument.** ServiceTitan is quote-based,
per-seat, tiered by module — pricebook in one tier, mobile estimates in the next,
payroll and memberships in the third, plus implementation. **Here, a tenant who
adds four apprentices and a second van pays exactly what they paid last month**
unless they send more messages.

⚠️ **The one thing that does scale with crew size is usage** — more technicians
send more on-the-way texts. ⭐ **And that is honest and predictable**, because the
tenant can see the per-message cost and the meter tops itself up (§17.6) rather
than blocking a van at the kerb.

## 30A.2 ⭐ INTEGRATION — NO NEW CANONICAL ENTITIES

**The thirteen modules extend the graph. They do not fork it.**

| FSM concept | Where it lives |

| Customer | ⭐ **`Person`** |
| Property / site | ⭐ **`Location`** |

| Conversation with the customer | ⭐ **`Conversation`** — the same thread the agent used |
| What the AI knows about the equipment | ⭐ **`Fact`** |

**Module-owned supporting tables** — legitimate, because none duplicates a
canonical noun: `PriceBookItem` · `PriceBookVersion` · `EstimateOption` ·
`Membership` · `MembershipVisit` · `InventoryItem` · `StockLocation` ·
`TimeEntry` · `Equipment` · `CommissionRule` · `SyncMapping`.

⛔ **`Equipment` attaches to `Location`, never to `Person`** — *the boiler stays
with the house when the customer moves, which is the correct model and the one
every trades business actually needs.*

## 30A.4 THE EVENT WIRING

**34 new events, every one with declared subscribers** *(build check ①, §13.8)*:

```
  estimate.approved ──► job.create · deposit.request · parts.reserve · commission.accrue
  membership.sold   ──► visits.generate · renewal.schedule · priority.flag
  job.completed     ──► invoice.generate · review.invite · costing.close ·
                        photos→content · attribution.close · commission.finalise ·
                        ⭐ inventory.deduct · timesheet.close
  inventory.low     ──► reorder.suggest · dispatch.flag

```

⭐ **`job.completed` now has eight subscribers and still requires no
coordination** — the event bus was built for exactly this, so adding an FSM
module is a subscription, not an integration.

## 30A.5 ⭐ THE SEVEN SEAMS THAT MATTER

| Seam | Direction · invalidation |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ `pricebook → agent` | one-way. **Price version bump invalidates the Fact in the same transaction** (§13.4) |
| `pricebook → site` | one-way. Page renders the row; ⛔ **never a copied number** |
| `pricebook → costing` | one-way. A job keeps ⭐ **the price version it was sold at** |
| `dispatch → timesheet` | one-way, derived. ⭐ *The timesheet and the schedule cannot disagree because one produces the other* |
| `job → sync` | one-way out. Idempotent. Conflicts surfaced (§30.5) |
| `photo → content` | one-way. ⭐ Deleting the photo removes the derived asset |
| `equipment → field assistant` | read-only. Invalidated when a job updates the equipment record |

  W4  X-169 Payroll  X-170 Commissions   need timesheets + job costing

```

# ══════════════════════════════════════════
# §31 · M8a — SEO I  *(EXECUTED T488)*
**Crawling & indexing (21) · speed (12) · content (18)**
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **⛔ FIRST-PASS SHAPE — PRECEDENCE (T667, §0.A):** first-pass SEO I; current §142 (M18). *Nothing here is deleted (law 10); read §0.A before treating this section as current.*

## 31.0 ⭐⭐ RESEARCH — THE AI-CRAWLER FINDING IS BIGGER THAN THE HARVEST SAID

The capability list called AI-crawler access *"the commonest AEO failure, usually
accidental."* **The research says it is far worse than that, and that we are
uniquely placed to fix it.**

### ⛔ THE FACTS

1. ⭐ **Since 1 July 2025, every new Cloudflare domain blocks GPTBot, ClaudeBot and
   PerplexityBot by default** — part of Content Independence Day, applying to
   **roughly 20% of the public web.**
2. ⛔ **"Block AI bots" does not distinguish training crawlers from retrieval
   crawlers. It blocks both.** *If OAI-SearchBot cannot reach your pages, ChatGPT
   Search stops citing you.*
3. ⭐ **~27% of B2B SaaS and ecommerce sites are accidentally blocking major LLM
   crawlers at the CDN layer** — while their own robots.txt says allow.
4. ⭐ **Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control prepends a managed block list to
   `/robots.txt` before it reaches crawlers**, so the tenant's file says one thing
   and the crawler sees another.
5. Per OpenAI: *"Sites opted out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT
   search answers."* ⭐ **Training and retrieval are independent systems.**

### ⭐ THE DISTINCTION THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING

| Bot | Job | Blocking it means |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **GPTBot** | OpenAI **training** | you're not in future models |
| ⭐ **OAI-SearchBot** | OpenAI **retrieval** | ⛔ **you vanish from ChatGPT Search** |
| **ClaudeBot** | Anthropic training | not in future models |
| ⭐ **Claude-SearchBot · Claude-User** | Anthropic retrieval | ⛔ **you vanish from Claude's answers** |
| **PerplexityBot** | retrieval | ⛔ you vanish from Perplexity |
| ⭐ **Google-Extended** | Gemini training **only** | ⭐ **the one cleanly free lever — blocking it does not affect Google Search ranking** |

⚠️ **Two traps worth naming.** `Claude-Web` and `anthropic-ai` are **deprecated** —
a site blocking only those is not blocking anything current. And Perplexity was
delisted from Cloudflare's Verified Bots in August 2025 over undeclared crawlers
that rotate user-agents and IPs; **as of early 2026 they are being rehabilitated,
but some zones still inherit a network-level reputation block** — so an allow rule
can look broken when it isn't.

### ⭐⭐ WHY THIS IS OURS TO WIN

> *"Verify your CDN is not silently overriding it. **This is the step most teams
> skip — and it accounts for the largest share of accidental AI invisibility.**"*

**Two layers must agree, and almost nobody checks both.**

⭐ **We provision Cloudflare for every tenant site (§26.3). We own both layers.**
So we can *guarantee* the robots.txt and the CDN agree — and prove it by fetching
as each bot and showing the response.

**→ NEW MODULE X-176 `AiCrawlerAccess`.**

---

## 31.1 ⭐ X-176 `AiCrawlerAccess` *(NEW)*

| Capability | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Two-layer audit** | robots.txt **and** the CDN/WAF, checked separately and compared |
| ⭐ **Fetch-as-bot** | request each user agent and **record the actual response code** — not what the config claims |
| **Per-bot policy** | training vs retrieval, chosen per bot, defaulted sensibly |
| ⭐ **Default: allow every retrieval bot** | *AI referrals are high-intent and growing; invisibility there is the expensive mistake* |
| **Training is the tenant's call** | Google-Extended flagged as ⭐ **free to block** — no ranking cost |
| **Deprecated-string check** | flags `Claude-Web` / `anthropic-ai` as doing nothing |
| **Cloudflare-specific** | verifies *"Manage your robots.txt"* is off so the origin file wins |
| ⭐ **Load guard** | a single bot over **5% of origin requests** → per-IP rate limit suggested |
| **Continuous** | re-checked weekly — ⭐ *a CDN default can change under them without warning* |

⭐ **The report a tenant sees:** *"ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity can all read your
site. Google's Gemini training crawler is blocked, which costs you nothing.
Checked 20 minutes ago."*

---

## 31.2 GROUP A — CRAWLING & INDEXING *(21)*

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **A1** robots.txt audit — ⭐ **and we serve it, so we can fix it** | **A2** ⭐ AI-crawler access → **X-176** |
| **A3** meta-robots + `X-Robots-Tag` on the **rendered** page — *a `noindex` left after a redesign is the classic silent killer* | **A4** canonical audit — self-reference, cross-domain, conflicts |
| **A5** ⭐ **index coverage from three sources** — Search Console, our sitemap, **the pixel's real page list**. *Three sources disagreeing is how you find pages Google cannot see* | **A6** orphan pages — in the sitemap, never linked, never visited |

### ⭐ 31.4.1 C8 AND C12 ARE THE TWO ONLY WE CAN DO

**C8 — FAQ from the inbox.** Every competitor guesses at FAQ or scrapes

and texts (§23.2). *The FAQ writes itself from what customers really asked, in
their words.*

**C12 — content decay.** Decay is normally measured in rankings or traffic. ⭐
**We measure it in `Asset.earns_calls`** (§11.7) — *"this page used to produce two
calls a week and hasn't produced one since June."* **A page can hold its ranking
and stop earning, and only we can see that.**

## 32.1 ⭐ RESEARCH — WHAT THE GBP API ACTUALLY PERMITS

| ✅ The API can | ⛔ It cannot |
| :--- | :--- |
| Create and update locations · hours and **special hours** · attributes · categories | Be used to prospect **other people's** businesses |
| Upload and remove media | Bypass verification |
| ⭐ **Publish posts** — offers, events, updates. **1,500 chars, one JPG/PNG, CTA buttons** *(Learn More · Book · Order · Shop · Sign Up · Call)* | |
| ⭐ **Fetch and reply to reviews** — list across locations, reply, delete replies, review media, reply status | |
| Fetch Q&A · pull performance insights — views, searches, customer actions | |

**Free to call. The constraint is access, not cost.**

### ⛔ 32.1.1 THE LEAD-TIME RISK — AND WHY ZERNIO IS THE ANSWER

> ⭐ **Every new Google Cloud project starts with ZERO quota.** A formal access
> request is required, demonstrating a legitimate use case, **a verified GBP
> active for 60+ days**, and a valid business website. **Approval takes time —
> sometimes weeks.**

**And the shape underneath it:** Google split GBP into **five separate APIs** —
in practice a federated model with different base URLs, OAuth scopes and rate
limits per surface.

⭐ **This is a not-in-our-control lead-time item**, the same class as carrier
approval or the demo number. **It has to be started early or it becomes the
critical path.**

✅ **Zernio is the answer, and it is why we have it.** It gives one endpoint,
handles the OAuth, the location management and *"all the GBP quirks"* — and by
its own account saves **4–6 weeks of development**. Sixteen platforms, one API.

**So: Zernio is the primary GBP path; the direct API is the complement** for
anything Zernio doesn't cover, with our own access request filed in parallel so
the fallback exists before it is needed.

### ⭐ 32.1.2 TWO BUILD RULES FROM THE RESEARCH

⛔ **Precise `updateMask` values, always.** *Passing `storefrontAddress` as the
mask touches only address fields, leaving hours, categories and attributes
untouched.* **A bulk update with a loose mask silently overwrites things nobody
asked to change** — and across a location portfolio that is very hard to notice
and very expensive to undo.

⛔ **Never partial CSV uploads for updates.** They *"repeatedly cause
cross-location data drift."* CSV is for one-off additions; **updates go through
the API.**

## 32.2 ⭐ X-177 `GbpGuardian` — SUSPENSION IS THE CATASTROPHE *(NEW)*

**A hard suspension removes the profile from Search and Maps entirely.** For a
local business that is the lights going out — and GBP is ~32% of local ranking
weight.

| | Soft suspension | Hard suspension |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Effect** | posts disappear · messaging disabled · **profile stays visible** while Google re-reviews | ⛔ **removed from Search and Maps** |

### ⭐ Prevention — the four documented causes, each checked continuously

| Cause | Our guard |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Address verification failure** | address consistency across GBP, site, citations and the `Location` record |
| **Category–storefront mismatch** | ⭐ flags a category that doesn't match the premises type — *a common accidental cause* |
| **Multiple profiles claiming one address** | duplicate detection across the fleet and the wider index |
| ⭐ **Keyword-stuffed business name** | ⛔ **we refuse to write one.** The name field renders the legal business name; *stuffing it is the single most common self-inflicted suspension* |

### ⭐ Preparation — the reinstatement pack, assembled before it's needed

Reinstatement needs **dated exterior signage photos, a utility bill or lease
matching the listed address, and a written explanation of recent changes.**

⭐ **We assemble it at onboarding, not at the emergency** — signage photos from
the tech's mobile uploads (§30.4), the address record, and a change log we
already keep (§12.6). *When a suspension lands, the pack is one click, and the
explanation writes itself from the actual change history.*

**Plus:** profile-change monitoring, so ⭐ **an unauthorised edit or a Google-applied
change is caught the day it happens**, not at the next audit.

### X-144 — the mechanics

Ask the assistants the queries that matter **on a schedule**, across ChatGPT,
Perplexity, Google AI Mode, Claude, Gemini and Copilot. Record whether the
business is named, ⭐ **and keep the answer verbatim with its date.**

Metrics: citation frequency · share of voice · citation position · answer
sentiment · query coverage by intent · AI referral traffic.

⚠️ **Two honest notes.** ⭐ **AI answers are geo-personalised**, so a query must be
run from the tenant's own market to mean anything — we run from the service area,
not from a datacentre. And the results are **a sample, not a census**; the report
says so, and shows the query set.

⭐ **Profound charges $399/mo for three engines. We include six** — and because
we already run a proxy pool (§18A.2), running from the right geography costs us
nothing extra.

## 32.7 ⭐ THE THREE LOOPS — SEO COMPLETE

```
  ① THE CONVERSATION LOOP    inbox ──► FAQ ──► page ──► answer engine
       every question a customer asked becomes content that answers the next one

  ② THE JOB LOOP             job done ──► photo + review + GBP post + location proof

  ③ THE MONEY LOOP           page ──► call ──► job ──► invoice ──► which SEO work paid
       ⭐ the only loop that closes, and it closes because of S1
```

⭐ **X-140 `ConversationToContent` is loop ①**, and it is the one the research said
nobody ships: the transcripts already exist, and nobody mines them. **We turn
what customers actually asked into the FAQ, the page copy, the GBP Q&A and the
schema** — in their words, not a keyword tool's.

# §33 · ⭐ THE COMPLETENESS CHECK — FOUR DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED *(T490)*
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **🗄️ HISTORICAL — PRECEDENCE (T667, §0.A):** completeness check T490. *Nothing here is deleted (law 10); read §0.A before treating this section as current.*

**Law 7: every claim greppable, completeness checked never asserted.** The check
was run rather than the claim made, and it found four real defects.

## 33.1 ⛔ DEFECT 1 (worst) — X-157 WAS ASSIGNED TO THREE MODULES

⛔ **A direct violation of law 2** — a module's number never changes, and one
number can never mean three things.

| Was | Cause | ✅ Now |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **X-157** = `HostingEdge` *(§25A.4)* | first assignment | ✅ **X-157 `HostingEdge`** — earliest wins |
| **X-157** = `AiDesigner` *(§26.2)* | second write of §26 | ✅ **X-178 `AiDesigner`** |
| **X-157** = `TemplateMatcher` *(§26.4)* | third | ✅ **X-179 `TemplateMatcher`** |
| **X-158** = `TemplateMatcher` *(§26.3)* | collided with VideoEngine | ✅ **X-158 `VideoEngine`** keeps it *(whole section, §27)* |

⭐ **Minimal reassignment on purpose: two modules move to the end of the range,
nothing else cascades.** X-160 onward is untouched.

⭐ **Root cause, named so it doesn't repeat:** §26 was written **twice** across two
turns and both copies landed in the file. **The number register must be a
generated check, not a memory** — added to the build checks (§13.8) as ⑦:
*every `X-nnn` maps to exactly one module name.*

## 34.2 ⛔ THE PLACEHOLDER — X-180 `ContentPack` *(NEW)*

**A single file with a fixed schema, versioned, that the seeder parses. The
schema is built now; the file arrives later.**

```
CONTENT-PACK.md          ← the one file you and I author in a day or two
   │
   ├─ ═══ PROFILES ═══        200 blocks, uniform format
   ├─ ═══ TEMPLATES ═══       200 blocks (mostly generated, §25.2)
   ├─ ═══ LANDERS ═══         200 vertical pages, from PIII-18's skeleton
   ├─ ═══ ADS ═══             ad sets per vertical
   ├─ ═══ SEQUENCES ═══       outreach ladders, lifecycle sets
   └─ ═══ DOC PACKS ═══       six families × five docs
        │
        ▼
   ⭐ ONE SEEDER PARSES ALL OF IT
        │
        ├─► industry_profiles · profile_prices · profile_faqs
        ├─► page templates (block JSON)
        ├─► landers · ad_sets · message_templates · doc views
        └─► `Fact` rows, SAMPLE-badged until the tenant confirms
```

### ⭐ The uniform block format — why it matters

The nine `DE-*` files already use a **uniform `═══` delimiter format by design**,
which is what made the original seeder possible. ⭐ **The content pack extends the
same convention**, so:

- **The parser is written now**, against the format, with the 100 existing
  profiles as its test fixture.
- **Adding content is appending blocks.** No parser change, no migration, no
  schema negotiation.
- ⭐ **Antigravity's instruction is one line:** *"parse CONTENT-PACK.md with the
  seeder; everything else is already built."*

### The block schema

```
═══ PROFILE ═══
slug: emergency-plumber
family: home-trades
name: Summit Plumbing
tone: direct, reassuring, no jargon
─── PRICES ───
Drain clear | 85 | GBP | callout included
...8–15 rows
─── FAQ ───
Q: Do you charge for a callout?
A: ...
...10–15 rows
─── SAFETY ───
(required-review lines, 911/999-first where relevant)
═══ END ═══
```

⭐ **Same shape for landers, ads and sequences** — one delimiter convention across
every asset type, so one parser handles all six sections.

## 35.1 ⭐ THE DEMO NUMBER — PLACEHOLDER, AND O1 CLOSES

**`platform_settings.demo_number` ships with a placeholder value. Every one of
the 51 surfaces reads that key. Buying the real number is a one-line config
change with no deploy.**

```
demo_number: "[DEMO-NUMBER]"
      │
      ├─ 51 surfaces read the key, never a literal
      ├─ ⭐ SMS + chat demo paths work with NO number at all
      │     the six-family QR grid, the picker, the web chat — all live
      ├─ voice demo block renders but is FLAG-DARK until the key is real
      └─ swap = one config row ──► every surface fills at once
```

### ⭐ How the demo SMS system is built and tested without it

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Development** | a **test number** on the existing Infobip account — the same code path, a different value |
| **Automated tests** | the demo runs against a **loopback transport** that records instead of sends *(the existing demo-mode transports)* |
| ⭐ **Copy and QR assets** | authored with the placeholder token, **so nothing needs rewriting** — the token renders the real number the moment it exists |
| **Sanity check** | ⛔ **a build check fails if any surface hard-codes a number** instead of reading the key |
| **Go-live** | buy it · point the voice webhook · change one row |

⭐ **The demo engine is fully buildable and fully testable today.** The number is
a value, not a dependency — which was always the design intent, and is now
enforced by a check rather than remembered.

## 35.3 ⭐ GAP 1 — AUTOMATION SAFETY *(→ X-125 `AutomationCanvas`)*

**The research on Customer.io, Braze and Klaviyo surfaced four patterns for
letting an agent run a workflow safely. None were in the canvas spec.**

| Pattern | ✅ Now in X-125 |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Read-only "safe mode"** | A workflow runs **computing every action without executing any**, and shows exactly what it *would* have done. **Not a preview of one step — a full dry run over real data** |
| ⭐ **Auto-pause after N consecutive failures** | Default **3**. ⛔ *A workflow failing repeatedly is worse than one that stopped — it burns credits and trust simultaneously* |
| **Built-in simulation before publish** | Runs against the last 30 days of real events *(this is X-141 replay, §13.7, pointed at a draft)* |
| **Approve-then-autonomise per workflow** | The same ladder as the assistant (§14.1), scoped per workflow rather than globally |

⭐ **Safe mode is the one that matters.** *"Show me what this would have done to
my last 400 contacts"* is the difference between a tenant trusting an automation
and never turning it on — and **we get it nearly free, because replay already
exists.**

## 35.4 ⭐ GAP 2 — REGISTRY GOVERNANCE *(→ X-142 `McpServer`)*

Salesforce governs which MCP servers and tools are trusted, with rate limits per
tool. **Ours is the reverse position — we are the server — and it needs the same
discipline pointed outward.**

| ✅ Now in X-142 |
| :--- |
| ⭐ **Per-tool rate limits**, not just per-token — *one agent looping on `crm.contact.list` must not starve the tenant's own dashboard* |
| **Per-client action allowlists** — a connected agent gets a **subset**, not everything the user can do |
| ⭐ **Consent screen naming the actions**, not the scope — *"this can book jobs and send texts"* beats *"read/write access"* |
| **Revocation from the tenant's own screen**, effective on the next request *(the §17.1 pattern)* |
| ⭐ **Every MCP call is an `ActionInvocation` with `actor_type: mcp`** and the client id — so `EXPLAIN` can answer *"which agent did that?"* |

## 35.5 ⭐ GAP 3 — INTENT BRANCHING *(→ X-125)*

GoHighLevel's 2026 addition: **branch on the *meaning* of a customer message, not
on keywords.**

⭐ **We already have the classifier** (§16.5) — it runs on every inbound turn. So
an `intent` branch node costs almost nothing and replaces the brittle thing every
competitor ships:

```
  ⛔ keyword branch:  message contains "cancel"  ──► cancellation flow
                      *"I don't want to cancel, I want to reschedule"* → wrong flow

  ⭐ intent branch:   intent = reschedule ──► reschedule flow
                      intent = cancel     ──► retention flow
                      intent = complaint  ──► human, immediately
```

⛔ **And the honest limit, stated in the node itself:** intent classification is
**probabilistic**. The node shows its confidence, and ⭐ **a low-confidence branch
routes to the default path rather than guessing** — because a wrong branch on a
complaint is worse than an unbranched one.

# §36 · M9 — REVIEWS & REPUTATION  *(EXECUTED T495)*
⛔ **The research forced a design reversal. Read 36.0 before anything else.**
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

> **⛔⛔ SUPERSEDED — PRECEDENCE (T667, §0.A):** by §37 (the client QA system — owner law); reviews current at §148. *Nothing here is deleted (law 10); read §0.A before treating this section as current.*

## 36.0 ⛔⛔ SENTIMENT ROUTING IS NOW A LIABILITY — AND IT WAS IN OUR PLAN

**The standard review mechanic — survey first, route happy customers to Google,
unhappy ones to a private form — is called review gating, and 2026 changed
everything about it.**

| ⛔ What changed in 2026 | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Enforcement** | *"What changed in 2026 is that Google is now **actively detecting and enforcing** it."* |
| ⭐ **Retroactive** | *"Businesses that built their review profile using gating tactics are seeing those reviews removed **retroactively, including some left years ago**."* |
| **Silent** | ⭐ *"Google's automated systems remove non-compliant reviews **without notification**."* |
| **Collateral** | ⛔ *"Legitimate positive reviews have been caught in the sweeps — **service businesses like medical, dental and home services are losing a higher share** of positive reviews than other industries."* **That is our exact customer base.** |

### ⛔ The April 17 2026 update added two new bans

| New ban | Why it matters to us |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Asking customers to mention staff names** | *"For years companies trained staff to ask for specific mentions. It felt harmless and even helpful. Under the updated guidelines it is now **explicitly against the rules**."* |
| **Pressuring customers to review while on premises** | ⭐ **review kiosks, shared tablets and in-store review stations are now explicitly against policy** |
| Also banned | **review quotas** · asking for specific keywords |

**And the standing rules, now enforced with AI detection:** no incentives of any
kind *(including to revise or remove a negative review)* · no employee, vendor or
family reviews · ⭐ **sudden volume spikes can trigger removals** · US businesses
also carry FTC exposure.

### ⛔ SO §13.3'S `review.routed_private` IS STRUCK

**Our own event catalogue listed sentiment routing. It is removed.** This is the
same class of correction as *mini-Shopify* (§25.0) and *Calendly clone* (§29.0) —
**caught by research before it was built, which is the entire point of §7E.**

⭐ **Added to the kill list as item 22.**

---

## 36.1 ⭐ WHAT REPLACES IT — AND IT IS BETTER

> ⭐ **The difference is whether everyone gets asked — not whether you ask at
> all.** Google still wants businesses to collect reviews.

### ⭐ The parallel path, not the filter

```
  ⛔ GATING (dead)                    ⭐ OURS (parallel, and better)

  job done                            job done
     │                                   │
  satisfaction survey                 ⭐ EVERY customer, same message,
     │                                   same timing, within 24h
  happy? ──yes──► Google                 │
     │                                   ├──► the review link
     no                                  │
     │                                   └──► ⭐ "or tell us privately if
  private form only                            anything wasn't right"
                                               — offered to EVERYONE
```

⭐ **Nobody is routed by sentiment. Everyone gets both.** And it produces
something gating never could: ⭐ **private feedback from happy customers too** —
the *"great job, but the van blocked my neighbour's drive"* that never reaches a
business whose unhappy-only form is the sole private channel.

### ⭐ "ASK FOR STORIES, NOT STARS"

The single most useful line in the research, and it is a **double win**:

> ⭐ *"Reviews that mention the specific service, the neighbourhood and the
> outcome **survive AI filtering far better** than generic 'Great service!'
> praise — and **they convert better too**."*

**So the request names the job, never the words:**

| ⭐ We prompt | ⛔ We never prompt |
| :--- | :--- |
| *"How did the boiler repair go?"* | *"Mention Dave"* — ⛔ **banned April 2026** |
| *"What did we sort out for you?"* | *"Say emergency plumber Croydon"* — ⛔ keyword stuffing |
| the service, from the `Job` record | a star rating target — ⛔ quotas banned |

⭐ **The job record already knows the service, the date and the address**, so the
prompt is specific without ever telling the customer what to write. *We supply
the context; they supply the words.*

---

## 36.2 ⭐ X-181 `ReviewIntegrity` — THE GUARD *(NEW)*

⛔ **Reviews are the most valuable trust asset a local business has, they live
entirely on Google's servers, and they can vanish on a Tuesday.** This module
exists because of that sentence.

| Guard | Behaviour |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⛔ **No sentiment routing, structurally** | there is **no code path** that sends a different link based on a rating. *Not a setting — an absence* |
| ⭐ **Spike detection** | volume spikes trigger removals, so the sender **paces itself**: a backlog of 200 completed jobs releases over days, never in one batch |
| ⭐ **Prompt lint** | the request template is checked for staff names, keywords, star targets and incentive language — ⛔ **and refuses to send if it finds them** |
| **Reply lint** | ⛔ replies checked for promotional language, keyword stuffing and post-review offers — **all banned in replies too** |
| **Insider detection** | flags a review from a known staff, vendor or family contact **before** it becomes a violation |
| ⛔ **No kiosk mode** | we do not build one. *Explicitly against policy since 2026* |
| ⭐ **REVIEW LOSS DETECTION** | ⭐ **daily count per destination. A drop is an alert** — *"you had 47 Google reviews on Monday, you have 41 today"* |
| **Pause detection** | Google paused submissions on flagged profiles in July 2026 — ⭐ **we detect the pause and stop sending**, rather than pushing requests into a wall |

⭐ **Review loss detection is the one nobody ships.** Google removes silently, and
a business finds out weeks later by accident. **We tell them the next morning** —
and because we hold every review's text and date (§23), ⭐ **we can show them
exactly which ones went.**

---

## 36.3 THE REVIEW ENGINE

| Capability | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Trigger** | `job.completed` → request **within 24 hours** *(highest response rates)*, at a sensible local hour |
| **Channel** | SMS by default *(RCS where verified, §15.4)*, email fallback |
| **Everyone** | ⛔ **no filtering, no exclusions, no quotas** |
| **Destinations** | Google first — ⭐ **79.4% of all reviews per location** — then the industry's second platform from the profile |
| **Follow-up** | ⭐ **one** reminder, and only if unopened. *Two is pressure* |
| **Multi-location** | per-location profiles, per-location paces |
| ⭐ **The agent can ask** | on a call, in the natural place — *"would you mind leaving us a review? I'll text you the link"* |

### AI replies — with the 2026 constraints built in

Draft within **60 seconds** *(the §7D benchmark, against Birdeye's 2–3 minutes)*,
in the tenant's brand voice, ⛔ **linted for promotional language and keyword
stuffing before it can post.** Negative reviews route to a human by default with a
draft prepared. ⭐ **A reply signals a monitored, legitimate profile** — which is
itself a positive signal.

### Distribution and use

⭐ **Review text is a content asset** (§32.3 E8): mined into page copy, FAQ and
GBP services, ⭐ **tagged by service and town**, rendered as schema, published to
the site gallery and social. **One review, five destinations.**

### ⭐ Recovery, not suppression

A bad review arrives → the tenant is alerted with context *(the job, the tech, the
transcript)* → a draft reply → ⭐ **and the private-feedback path that was always
offered means the customer often used it first**, giving the business a chance to
fix it before it was ever public. ⛔ **That is not gating — the public link was
offered at the same moment, to the same person.**

# §37 · ⭐⭐ THE CLIENT QA SYSTEM — OWNER LAW  *(T496 · SUPERSEDES §36.0–36.2)*

> ⭐⭐⭐ **[RE-AMENDED T677 — OWNER · §168A · this supersedes the §168.0.1 banner] THE GATE LIVES, AS A TENANT PREFERENCE — AND IT IS A SEQUENCE, NOT A FILTER.** `public_threshold` default 4 *(1–3 gated, unchanged)*, max 5. ⭐ **The loop is the law: gated → the ticket and its SLA → RESOLVED → the AI asks again → at or above the ungated level the public link goes out normally.** `fix_then_ask_enabled` flips **ON** and fires on `ticket.resolved`, never a timer. The public review then goes to the tenant's own destination roster *(Google · Yelp · Facebook · BBB · Bing · Trustpilot · app store)* — inferred, confirmed once, distributed unasked. ⛔ **Everything else in this section stands exactly as written and nothing is deleted (law 10).** *Read §168A.*
# ══════════════════════════════════════════

## 37.1 ⭐ THE LAW

> **Every review request is TRIAGED. Low ratings go to internal QA. High ratings
> are asked for a public review.**
>
> ⭐ **The purpose is to look after the client and fix anyone with an issue.**
> This is a **quality assurance system**, and the public review is the by-product
> of doing the job well.

⛔ **§36.0's reversal is void. §36.1's parallel-path-only design is void.**
Triage is the design and it does not change.

**What stays from §36 — it was good work and none of it depended on the
reversal:** stories-not-stars prompting · no staff-name or keyword asks · spike
pacing · reply lint · ⭐ **review loss detection** · submission-pause detection ·
24-hour timing · one reminder.

## 37.2 ⭐ X-181 RENAMED — `ClientQa`

**The framing was wrong and the rename fixes it.** This is not a review-policy
module. **It is the internal quality system for the tenant's business**, and
review requests are one of its outputs.

```
  job completed
       │
  ⭐ QA CHECK — "How did we do?"          ← the tenant's own quality gate
       │
       ├─ 4–5 ★ ──► ⭐ "Would you share that publicly?" → review link
       │
       └─ 1–3 ★ ──► ⭐⭐ A REAL SUPPORT TICKET
                        │
                        ├─ routed to a human, with an SLA
                        ├─ the job · the tech · the transcript · the history attached
                        ├─ tracked to RESOLUTION, not to acknowledgement
                        └─ ⭐ closed back to the customer: "here's what we did"
```

⭐ **The low-rating path is the important half**, and it is where every competitor
stops. **Birdeye and Podium route unhappy customers to a form and consider the
job done.** ⛔ **A form is not a fix.** Ours opens a ticket, assigns it, times it,
and closes the loop with the customer.

---

## 37.3 ⭐ THE FIVE IMPROVEMENTS YOU ASKED FOR

### ⭐⭐ ① FIX-THEN-ASK — the highest-converting review request there is

```
  1–3★ ──► ticket ──► resolved ──► ⭐ 7 days later: "Did we get that sorted?"
                                        │
                                        └─ yes ──► ⭐ NOW ask for the review
```

⭐ **A customer whose complaint was actually fixed is the most enthusiastic
reviewer a business can have** — and they write the best reviews, because they
have a *story*: *"had a problem, they sorted it in a day."*

⛔ **Nobody does this.** Everyone treats a low rating as a leak to plug. ⭐ **It is
the best review you never asked for**, and it turns the QA system into a
*generator* rather than a filter.

### ⭐⭐ ② THE QA REPORT — worth more to the tenant than the reviews

**Every QA response is data about their business.** Aggregate it:

| The report says | From |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ *"Three customers this month mentioned the same scheduling problem"* | recurring themes across tickets |
| *"Dave's jobs average 4.9. Mike's average 4.1 — and it's always timekeeping"* | ⭐ per-technician quality, from the `Job` link |
| *"Your Tuesday jobs score lower than any other day"* | pattern by day, service, area |
| *"Callout-fee surprise is your most common complaint"* | ⭐ theme extraction from the free-text |
| *"Resolved tickets convert to 5★ reviews 68% of the time"* | the fix-then-ask loop, measured |

⭐ **This is the management report a small business has never had.** ServiceTitan
gives them job costing; nobody gives them *why customers are unhappy, ranked.*

### ③ THE QA STEP IS A REAL SURVEY, NOT A RATING GATE

⭐ **Ask a question worth answering**, so the response has value even at 5★:

> *"How did the boiler repair go? Anything we could have done better?"*

- **Free text on every rating**, not just low ones — ⭐ *the 5★ comment is where
  the marketing copy comes from.*
- One screen, no login, works in the SMS thread.
- The service name comes from the `Job` record, so it's specific.

### ④ THE INTERNAL RECORD IS PERMANENT AND SEARCHABLE

Every QA response is a `Message` on the `Conversation` (§11.5), joined to the
`Job`, the technician and the `Person`. ⭐ **So when that customer calls again in
two years, the agent knows there was an issue and that it was fixed** — which is
exactly the context a good business would have and never does.

### ⭐ ⑤ TWO THINGS TO AVOID — CHEAP, AND UNRELATED TO TRIAGE

⭐ **These are worth doing regardless, because they're free and they're distinct
bans that catch people out:**

| Avoid | Why it's cheap |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⛔ **Asking customers to mention a staff name** | banned April 2026 and **easy to do by accident** — the prompt lint catches it. *Say "how did the repair go", never "mention Dave"* |
| ⛔ **Asking for specific keywords** | same lint, same cost: zero |
| ⛔ **On-premises kiosks / shared review tablets** | we simply don't build one |
| ⭐ **Volume spikes** | ⭐ **the pacing already handles it** — and spikes trigger removals *regardless* of how reviews were collected, so this protects everyone |

---

## 37.4 ⚠️ THE ONE RISK, STATED ONCE

**So it's on the record and then we build:** Google's Maps UGC policy treats
pre-screening by sentiment as prohibited, enforcement became active in 2026, and
removals are **retroactive and silent**. Service businesses have been losing
legitimate positive reviews in the sweeps.

⭐ **What reduces exposure without changing your design at all:**

| Lever | Effect |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⭐ **Pacing** *(already built)* | spikes are a detection signal independent of triage |
| ⭐ **Stories not stars** *(already built)* | specific reviews survive filtering better |
| ⭐ **Fix-then-ask** *(new, §37.3①)* | ⭐ **it routes a low-rating customer back to the public link after resolution — so over time, more customers are asked, not fewer** |
| ⭐ **Loss detection** *(already built)* | ⭐ **if it ever happens, you know the next morning and can see which ones went** |

⭐ **`review_triage_mode` is a tenant setting**, defaulting to **TRIAGE**. An
agency or a nervous client can switch to `PARALLEL` *(both links, one message)*
without a code change — **the engine supports both because it's one config row.**

⛔ **Decision recorded, risk recorded, and it's yours.** Nothing else in the plan
waits on it.

---

## 37.5 WHAT §37 CHANGES

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| ⛔ **Reversed** | §36.0's strike · §36.1's parallel-only design · kill-list item 22 |
| ⭐ **Renamed** | X-181 `ReviewIntegrity` → ⭐ **`ClientQa`** |
| ⭐ **Added** | **fix-then-ask** · **the QA report** · real tickets with SLA and resolution · free text on every rating · permanent searchable QA history |
| **Kept from §36** | stories-not-stars · prompt lint · reply lint · pacing · loss detection · pause detection · 24h timing |
| **Events** | + `qa.response_received` · `qa.ticket_opened` · ⭐ `qa.resolved` · ⭐ `qa.review_requested_post_fix` · `qa.theme_detected` |
| **Modules** | **256 — no change**, X-181 renamed and expanded |

⭐ **The sentence this earns, and it's a better one than the compliance framing:**
*"We ask every customer how we did. If something went wrong we open a ticket, fix
it, and tell them what we did — and then we ask them to share it. If it went
well, we ask straight away."*

**That is a quality system that produces reviews, rather than a review system
that avoids complaints.**


---

## 37.6 ⭐ THE QA SETTINGS — OWNER RULING *(T497)*

**Every part is a tenant setting. Defaults stated; all changeable, none require a
deploy.**

| Setting | Default | Range |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `triage_enabled` | ⭐ **ON** | on / off — *off sends everyone the public link* |
| ⭐ `public_threshold` | **4★** | **1–5.** *A tenant who only wants 5★ going public sets 5. A tenant who wants everything sets 1* |
| ⭐ `fix_then_ask_enabled` | ⭐⭐ **ON** *(flipped by the owner, §168A)* | on / off — **it is the design; it fires on `ticket.resolved`, not on `fix_then_ask_delay`** |
| ~~`fix_then_ask_delay`~~ | ⛔ **MOOT (§168A)** | the trigger is `ticket.resolved` — *a delay guesses when the problem is fixed; the ticket knows* |
| `pacing_enabled` | ⭐ **ON** | on / off |
| `pacing_max_per_day` | auto | auto or fixed |
| `reminder_count` | 1 | 0–2 |
| `request_delay_hours` | 24 | 1–168 |

⭐ **`public_threshold` is the one that matters** — it is the whole triage rule as
a single number the tenant controls. **4 by default, theirs to move.**

⭐ **Fix-then-ask ships off.** It's built and ready; a tenant switches it on when
they want it, and the QA report will show them what it's worth once they do.
